questions.stem: A researcher investigated two species of mites: a predator and its prey. At the start of a week, there was an equal number of the two species. At the end of the week, the number of prey had increased by 2,700% of the number of prey at the start of the week, and the number of predators had increased by 180% of the number of predators at the start of the week. The number of prey at the end of the week was \(p\%\) greater than the number of predators at the end of the week. What is the value of \(p\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Since the two species start equal, call each starting count \(N\). "Increased by 2,700%" means the increase is added on: prey end at \(N(1 + 27) = 28N\), and predators end at \(N(1 + 1.8) = 2.8N\). "\(p\%\) greater than" compares the difference to the predators: \(\frac{28N - 2.8N}{2.8N} = \frac{25.2}{2.8} = 9\), which is 900%. So \(p = 900\).

questions.stem: A right rectangular prism has a base area of \(16t\) square centimeters (cm²). The length of the base of the rectangular prism is \(\frac{8}{3}\) cm, and the height of the rectangular prism is 9 cm. Which expression represents the surface area, in cm², of the right rectangular prism?
questions.whyCorrect: Get the missing width first: the base area is length times width, so \(w = 16t \div \frac{8}{3} = 6t\). Surface area is two bases plus the four side faces: \(2(16t) + 2\left(\frac{8}{3}\cdot 9\right) + 2(6t \cdot 9) = 32t + 48 + 108t\), which is \(140t + 48\).

whyWrong.A: This treats the base as a square of side \(\frac{8}{3}\), so the side faces come out as \(4\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)(9) = 96\) and the two \(6t \times 9\) faces are lost.
whyWrong.C: This multiplies instead of divides when finding the width: \(16t \cdot \frac{8}{3} = \frac{128t}{3}\) gives side faces of \(768t + 48\), and \(768t + 32t = 800t\).
whyWrong.D: \(144t\) is the volume, base area times height \(16t \cdot 9\), not the surface area.

questions.stem: An object's speed is increasing at the rate of 12.1 meters per second squared. What is this rate, in miles per minute squared, rounded to the nearest tenth? (Use 1 mile = 1,609 meters.)
questions.whyCorrect: Divide by 1,609 to turn meters into miles, and multiply by \(60^2 = 3600\) because the seconds in the denominator are squared: \(\frac{12.1 \times 3600}{1609} \approx 27.07\), which rounds to 27.1.

whyWrong.A: This is \(\frac{12.1 \times 60}{1609}\) — the seconds converted once rather than squared.
whyWrong.C: Neither factor is applied in a way that matches the units; the correct value is about 27, and 133 corresponds to no consistent step.
whyWrong.D: This is \(\frac{12.1 \times 1609}{60}\): multiplying by 1,609 instead of dividing by it.

questions.note: This book repeats this metres-per-second-squared to miles-per-minute-squared item several times (#6, #11, #13, #14, #16) with only the number changed — place at most one per test.

questions.stem: A right square pyramid has a surface area of 75,264 square inches, which includes a base area of 36,864 square inches. What is the slant height, in inches, of this pyramid?
questions.whyCorrect: The base is a square of area 36,864, so its side is \(\sqrt{36{,}864}=192\) inches. Subtract the base from the total to get the lateral area: 75,264 − 36,864 = 38,400 square inches. That lateral area is four congruent triangles, each with base 192 and height equal to the slant height \(\ell\), so \(4\cdot\frac{1}{2}(192)\ell = 384\ell = 38{,}400\). Therefore \(\ell = 100\) inches.

questions.stem: A container has a volume of 0.84 cubic meters. Which of the following is closest to this volume, in quarts? (Note: 100.00 centimeters = 1 meter. Use 946.35 cubic centimeters = 1.00 quart.)
questions.whyCorrect: Volume conversions cube the length factor: one cubic meter is \(100^3 = 1{,}000{,}000\) cubic centimeters. So \(0.84\) cubic meters is \(840{,}000\) cubic centimeters. Divide by the size of a quart: \(\frac{840{,}000}{946.35} \approx 887.62\) quarts.

whyWrong.A: This divides 0.84 by 946.35-sized numbers without ever converting cubic meters to cubic centimeters.
whyWrong.B: This is \(\frac{0.84 \times 946.35}{100}\); it both multiplies by the quart size instead of dividing and applies the 100 only once.
whyWrong.C: This is \(0.84 \times 946.35\) — multiplying by the size of a quart rather than dividing by it, and skipping the cubic-centimeter conversion.

In the given figure, NP is the diameter of semicircle O. Angles Q, R, and S are right angles, and point P is the midpoint of NQ. If PQ = 52 feet and NS = 18 feet, the area of the figure can be expressed as \(a\pi + b\) square feet, where a and b are integers. What is the value of \(a - b\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Because P is the midpoint of NQ, \(NP = PQ = 52\), so \(NQ = 104\) and the semicircle has radius 26. The figure is the rectangle NQRS plus the semicircle: rectangle \(= 104 \cdot 18 = 1872\), semicircle \(= \frac{1}{2}\pi(26)^2 = 338\pi\). So \(a = 338\), \(b = 1872\), and \(a - b = -1534\). The trap is using 52 as the diameter instead of half of NQ.
questions.note: Figure: rectangle NQRS with N top-left, Q top-right, R bottom-right, S bottom-left; a semicircle with centre O sits on top of side NQ with diameter NP, P lying between O and Q on NQ. Answer is negative because b is much larger than a.

questions.stem: The volume of a right rectangular prism with a square base is 2,448 cubic centimeters. If the area of the square base is 144 square centimeters, what is the area, in square centimeters, of one of the four lateral faces of the prism?
questions.whyCorrect: Volume = (base area)(height), so the height is 2,448 ÷ 144 = 17 cm. The square base has area 144, so each side is \(\sqrt{144}=12\) cm. A single lateral face is a rectangle whose sides are one base edge and the height: 12 × 17 = 204 square centimeters. The trap is stopping at the height or reporting all four faces at once.

whyWrong.A: This is the height of the prism, 2,448 ÷ 144. You still have to multiply it by the 12 cm base edge to get a face's area.
whyWrong.C: No step here produces 540. If you got it, check that you divided the volume by the base area (144) to get the height, not by the base edge or the perimeter.
whyWrong.D: This is the combined area of all four lateral faces, 4 × 204. The question asks for one of them.

questions.stem: A right square pyramid has a height of 11 centimeters (cm). A second right square pyramid has a height of 22 centimeters. The area of the bases of each of the two pyramids is 100 cm<sup>2</sup>. Which of the following is closest to the difference in the surface area of the second pyramid and the surface area of the first pyramid, in cm<sup>2</sup>?
questions.whyCorrect: Each base is a square of area 100, so each base edge is 10 cm and the two bases cancel out of the difference — only the lateral areas differ. The slant height of a right square pyramid is \(\sqrt{h^{2}+\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)^{2}}\), using half the base edge, so the slant heights are \(\sqrt{11^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{146}\approx 12.083\) and \(\sqrt{22^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{509}\approx 22.561\). Lateral area is \(4\cdot\frac{1}{2}(10)\ell = 20\ell\), so the difference is \(20(22.561-12.083)\approx 209.6\), closest to 209.

whyWrong.B: This is what you get by using the pyramid's height, 11 and 22, directly as the slant height: 20(22 − 11) = 220. The slant height runs up the middle of a triangular face and is always longer than the vertical height.
whyWrong.C: This is the difference in volumes, \(\frac{1}{3}(100)(22-11)\approx 366.7\), not surface areas.
whyWrong.D: This is the surface area of the second pyramid on its own, \(100+20\sqrt{509}\approx 551\). You still have to subtract the first pyramid's surface area.

questions.stem: In the figure, parallel lines r and s are intersected by lines t, u, and w. If d = 42, g = 143, and h > d, which statement about j and p must be true?
questions.whyCorrect: Work with the angle each slanted line makes with the horizontal parallel lines. Because r and s are parallel, the angle a line makes at r is the same angle it makes at s, so h describes the tilt of line u and d describes the tilt of line w, while g describes the tilt of line t. Where two slanted lines meet, the angle between them is the difference of their tilts: \(j = g - h = 143 - h\) and \(p = g - d = 143 - 42 = 101\). Since h > 42, subtracting h takes away more than subtracting 42 does, so \(j \lt 101 = p\).

whyWrong.A: This would require h = d. You are told h > d, which is exactly the condition that forces the two angles apart.
whyWrong.B: p is already 101 on its own, so \(j+p\) cannot be 90 for any positive j.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the inequality. A larger h means a steeper line u relative to t, which makes the angle between them smaller, not larger.

questions.note: Figure needed: horizontal parallel lines r (upper) and s (lower). Line t descends steeply left-to-right, line u ascends steeply left-to-right, and they cross above r with angle j marked in the upward-opening region between them. g is marked at t's intersection with r, in the region above r and right of t. h is marked at u's intersection with s, above s and right of u. Line w ascends left-to-right on the right side; d is marked at its intersection with r, above r and right of w. Lines t and w cross below s, with p marked in the downward-opening region between them.
questions.imageAlt: Two horizontal parallel lines r and s cut by three slanted lines t, u and w; five of the angles formed are labelled with variables.

questions.stem: The function \[ f(x) = 70{,}000(2)^{\frac{t}{820}} \] gives the number of bacteria in a population t minutes after an initial observation. How much time, in minutes, does it take for the number of bacteria in the population to double?
questions.whyCorrect: The population doubles when the factor \( 2^{\frac{t}{820}} \) equals 2, which happens when the exponent equals 1 — that is, when t = 820 minutes. In a model written as \( a \cdot 2^{\frac{t}{k}} \) , the number k under the t is the doubling time.

whyWrong.A: This is the base of the exponent, the factor the population grows by, not the time it takes.
whyWrong.C: This is two doubling periods, after which the population is four times its original size.
whyWrong.D: This is the starting number of bacteria, not a time.

questions.note: The book writes the function as f(x) but uses t as the variable throughout; transcribed as printed.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((5x^{3} - 3x + 8) - (9x^{6} + 5x - 3)\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Distribute the minus sign: \(5x^{3} - 3x + 8 - 9x^{6} - 5x + 3\). Now combine: \(-9x^{6}\) stands alone, \(5x^{3}\) stands alone, \(-3x - 5x = -8x\), and \(8 + 3 = 11\).

whyWrong.A: \(-4x^{9}\) comes from subtracting \(9x^{6}\) from \(5x^{3}\) as though they were like terms; different powers never combine.
whyWrong.C: The signs on the second bracket's last two terms were not changed: \(-3x - 5x\) is \(-8x\), and \(8-(-3)\) is 11.
whyWrong.D: Both errors — the unlike powers were merged and the constants were subtracted instead of added.

questions.stem:
\[ 18x^2-24x+c=0 \]
In the given equation, \(c\) is a constant. The equation has exactly one solution. What is the value of \(c\) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Exactly one solution means the discriminant is zero: \((-24)^2-4(18)c=0\), so \(576=72c\) and \(c=8\). (Check: \(18x^2-24x+8=2(3x-2)^2\), a perfect square.)

questions.stem: \[ |x - 9| + 81 = 99 \]What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?
questions.whyCorrect: Isolate the absolute value: \( |x - 9| = 18 \), so \( x - 9 = 18 \) or \( x - 9 = -18 \), giving x = 27 and x = −9. Their sum is 18. There is a shortcut worth remembering: the two solutions always sit the same distance either side of 9, so their sum is 2(9) = 18 no matter what the right-hand side is.

questions.stem: The function h is defined by \( h(x) = a^{x} + b \) , where a and b are positive constants. The graph of y = h(x) in the xy-plane passes through the points \( (0, 10) \) and \( (2, 13) \) . What is the value of ab?
questions.whyCorrect: Use the point with x = 0 first, because \( a^{0} = 1 \) whatever a is: 1 + b = 10, so b = 9. Then the second point gives \( a^{2} + 9 = 13 \) , so \( a^{2} = 4 \) and a = 2 (a is positive). The product is ab = 2(9) = 18.

whyWrong.A: 13 is the y-coordinate of the second point, not the product.
whyWrong.C: 20 comes from b = 10, forgetting that \( a^{0} \) contributes 1 to the output.
whyWrong.D: 26 comes from a = 2 and b = 13, using the second point's y-value directly as b.

questions.stem:
3.5x + 1.2y = 8
17.5x + 6y = 40

How many solutions does the given system of equations have?
questions.whyCorrect: Look for a single scale factor connecting the two equations. From 3.5 to 17.5 the factor is 5; check the rest with the same 5: 1.2 × 5 = 6 and 8 × 5 = 40, both matching the second equation. All three parts scale identically, so the equations describe the same line and every point on it is a solution.

whyWrong.A: Exactly one solution requires the coefficient ratios to differ, but \(\frac{3.5}{17.5} = \frac{1.2}{6} = \frac{1}{5}\). The lines are not distinct, so they do not cross at a single point.
whyWrong.B: Two straight lines can meet at zero, one, or infinitely many points — never exactly two. This choice can be eliminated before doing any arithmetic.
whyWrong.D: Zero solutions would need the coefficients to scale by 5 while the constant did not. Here the constant scales by 5 too (8 × 5 = 40), so the lines coincide instead of being parallel.

questions.stem:
Which of the following expressions is (are) a factor of \( 4x^{2} + 31x - 45 \) ?
I. \( x - 9 \)
II. \( 4x - 5 \)
questions.whyCorrect: The expression factors as \( (4x - 5)(x + 9) \) : the cross terms are \( 36x \) and \( -5x \) , which combine to \( +31x \) . So II is a factor and the other factor is \( x + 9 \) , not \( x - 9 \) . A quick check for I: a factor \( x - 9 \) would mean x = 9 is a root, but substituting 9 gives \( 324 + 279 - 45 = 558 \) .

whyWrong.A: I has the wrong sign. Since the constant term is negative and the middle term is positive, the larger factor pairs with \( +9 \) .
whyWrong.C: Both cannot be factors: \( (x - 9)(4x - 5) \) expands to \( 4x^{2} - 41x + 45 \) , which has the wrong middle and constant terms.
whyWrong.D: Testing \( x = \frac{5}{4} \) gives \( 4(\frac{25}{16}) + 31(\frac{5}{4}) - 45 = 0 \) , so II really is a factor.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(2x^{3} + 8x^{2}y + xy^{2} + 4y^{3}\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Factor by grouping. The first pair gives \(2x^{2}(x + 4y)\) and the second pair gives \(y^{2}(x + 4y)\). Both share \((x+4y)\), so the expression is \((2x^{2} + y^{2})(x + 4y)\). If your grouping does not leave the same bracket twice, regroup.

whyWrong.A: Expanding gives \(2x^{3} + 2x^{2}y^{2} + 4xy + 4y^{3}\) — the two middle terms are wrong.
whyWrong.C: The degrees are too high; expanding produces \(x^{5}\) terms, which the original does not have.
whyWrong.D: Expanding gives \(2x^{4} + 8x^{3}y + xy^{3} + 4y^{4}\), one degree too high throughout.

questions.stem: Exactly how many x-intercepts does the graph of \( f(x) = x(x-8)^{2}(x-13)^{3} \) have in the xy-plane, where \( y = f(x) \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Set each factor to zero: x = 0, x = 8 and x = 13. That is three distinct values, so three x-intercepts. The exponents change how the curve behaves at each intercept — it touches and turns at x = 8 and flattens as it crosses at x = 13 — but every root is still a point where the graph meets the axis.

whyWrong.A: The function is zero at three different inputs, so it certainly meets the x-axis.
whyWrong.B: This counts only the plain x factor. The bracketed factors give roots too.
whyWrong.C: This drops the repeated root x = 8 on the grounds that the graph only touches the axis there. Touching the axis still counts as an intercept.

questions.stem:
\(F(x) = \frac{9}{5}(x - 273.15) + 32\)

The function \(F\) gives the temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, that corresponds to a temperature of \(x\) kelvins. If a temperature increased by 8.80 kelvins, by how much did the temperature increase, in degrees Fahrenheit?
questions.whyCorrect: The question asks about a change, not a temperature. In a linear function only the slope affects a change: adding 8.80 to \(x\) adds \(\frac{9}{5} \times 8.80 = 15.84\) to \(F\). The \(-273.15\) and the \(+32\) shift both readings equally and cancel out of the difference.

whyWrong.B: This is \(15.84 + 32\) — you kept the \(+32\) offset, but a constant added to both temperatures cancels when you subtract them.
whyWrong.C: This is \(F(8.80)\) with the \(+32\) dropped: you treated 8.80 as an absolute temperature in kelvins instead of an increase.
whyWrong.D: This is \(F(8.80)\), the Fahrenheit reading for 8.80 kelvins, not the size of the increase.

questions.stem: \[(v - 12)(v - 3) = 0\]What are all possible solutions to the given equation?
questions.whyCorrect: A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero. Setting \(v - 12 = 0\) gives \(v = 12\), and \(v - 3 = 0\) gives \(v = 3\). The solution makes the factor vanish, so the sign flips from what is written inside the parentheses.

whyWrong.A: \(-12\) comes from reading the factor \((v-12)\) as if it were \((v+12)\). Substituting \(-12\) gives \((-24)(-15) \ne 0\).
whyWrong.B: Neither value works: \(-12\) has the sign wrong and 9 appears nowhere in the equation.
whyWrong.C: Both signs are flipped. \(-3\) makes the factors \(-15\) and \(-6\), whose product is not zero.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the graph of 60x − 10y = −48 in the xy-plane?
questions.whyCorrect: Solve for y so the equation is in the form y = mx + b. From 60x − 10y = −48 you get −10y = −60x − 48, and dividing every term by −10 gives y = 6x + 4.8. The slope is the coefficient of x, so it is 6. Dividing by a negative flips the sign of the 60x term - that is the step most people miss.

whyWrong.A: −6 is what you get if you divide by 10 instead of −10, leaving the sign of the x term unchanged.
whyWrong.B: This is a ratio of the wrong two numbers and has the wrong sign.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{5}{4} \) comes from combining the constants rather than isolating y; it is not the coefficient of x in slope-intercept form.

questions.stem: For x = 0, y has a value of 200. The value of y increases by 40% for every increase of 1 in the value of x. Which equation represents this situation?
questions.whyCorrect: A fixed percentage increase per unit step is exponential growth, so the changing quantity has to be in the exponent, and the base is 1 plus the rate: 1 + 0.40 = 1.40. The 200 sits in front because it is the value at x = 0.

whyWrong.A: Here x is the base and 40 the exponent, which is a power function, not exponential growth. It also gives y = 0 at x = 0, contradicting the stated 200.
whyWrong.C: A base of 40 would multiply y by 40 each step, a 3,900% increase, not 40%.
whyWrong.D: Again x is in the base rather than the exponent, so y = 0 when x = 0.

questions.stem: A circle has diameters \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{BD}\). The circumference of the circle is \(84\pi\), and the length of arc \(DA\) is 2 times the length of arc \(AB\). What is the length of arc \(BC\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Two diameters cut the circle into four arcs, and arcs on opposite sides of the centre are equal because their central angles are vertical angles: arc \(BC\) = arc \(DA\) and arc \(AB\) = arc \(CD\). Since \(\overline{AC}\) is a diameter, arc \(AB\) + arc \(BC\) is half the circumference, \(42\pi\). Writing arc \(AB = x\), the condition arc \(DA = 2\,\text{arc}\,AB\) makes arc \(BC = 2x\) as well, so \(x + 2x = 42\pi\), \(x = 14\pi\), and arc \(BC = 28\pi\).

whyWrong.A: \(2\pi\) treats the "2 times" as a length in itself rather than a ratio.
whyWrong.B: \(14\pi\) is arc \(AB\), the smaller of the two arcs. Arc \(BC\) is twice that.
whyWrong.C: \(21\pi\) is a quarter of the circumference, which would only be right if the two diameters were perpendicular — that is, if all four arcs were equal.

questions.stem:
In the figure, parallel lines a and b are intersected by lines c, d, and e. If x = 49, y = 136, and v < z, which statement about x and w must be true?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.whyCorrect: Look for the two triangles that x and w each sit in. Line c cuts both parallel lines, so the angle it makes with b and the angle it makes with a are equal — and each of those triangles has that same angle, 180 - 136 = 44 degrees, as a second angle. In the triangle containing x, the third angle is v, so x = 180 - 44 - v = 136 - v. In the triangle containing w, the third angle is z, so w = 136 - z by exactly the same count. Since v < z, subtracting the smaller number leaves the larger result, so x > w. (As a check, x = 49 forces v = 87, and z must then exceed 87.)

whyWrong.A: This is the comparison you get by carrying v < z straight through to x and w, but both appear subtracted from 136, which flips the inequality.
whyWrong.C: x = w would require v = z, and the problem states v < z.
whyWrong.D: x + w = 136 - v + 136 - z = 272 - (v + z), which is only 90 if v + z = 182 — nothing in the problem forces that.

questions.stem: \[2\cos(90 - a)^\circ \cdot \cos b^\circ + \sin(a + y)^\circ \cdot \sin(90 - b)^\circ\]In the given expression, \(a\) and \(b\) are constants such that \(\sin a^\circ = 0.5\), \(\cos b^\circ = 0.99\), and \(0 < b < 90\). What is the value of the given expression when \(y = 0\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Use the cofunction identities rather than trying to find \(a\) and \(b\) themselves. \(\cos(90 - a)^\circ = \sin a^\circ = 0.5\) and \(\sin(90 - b)^\circ = \cos b^\circ = 0.99\). With \(y = 0\), \(\sin(a + y)^\circ = \sin a^\circ = 0.5\). The expression becomes \(2(0.5)(0.99) + (0.5)(0.99) = 0.99 + 0.495 = 1.485\).
questions.note: Answer 1.485 exactly; it fits a grid-in without rounding.

questions.stem:
\[ \frac{x+1}{5x^2}=\frac{k}{x} \]
In the given equation, \(k\) is a constant. The solution to the given equation is \(\frac{1}{224}\). What is the value of \(k\) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Cross multiply: \(x(x+1)=5kx^2\). Since \(x\ne 0\), divide by \(x\) to get \(x+1=5kx\), so \(1=x(5k-1)\) and \(x=\frac{1}{5k-1}\). Matching that to \(\frac{1}{224}\) gives \(5k-1=224\), so \(k=45\).

questions.stem: \[b - 49 = \frac{x}{y}\]The given equation relates the positive numbers \(b\), \(x\), and \(y\). Which equation correctly expresses \(x\) in terms of \(b\) and \(y\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(y\), letting it act on the whole left side: \(x = y(b - 49) = by - 49y\).

whyWrong.A: Multiplying and then dividing by \(y\) undoes the step; this is not equal to \(y(b-49)\).
whyWrong.C: Only \(b\) was multiplied by \(y\). The 49 is part of the same expression and must be multiplied as well.
whyWrong.D: Dividing by \(y\) goes the wrong way — \(x\) is already divided by \(y\) in the original equation.

questions.stem: The population of a certain city doubled every 75 years from 1651 to 1951. The population of this city was 160,000 in 1951. What was the population of this city in 1651?
questions.whyCorrect: Count the doublings first: 1951 − 1651 = 300 years, and 300 ÷ 75 = 4 doubling periods. So the 1951 population is the 1651 population multiplied by \( 2^{4} = 16 \) . Dividing back, \( 160{,}000 \div 16 = 10{,}000 \) .

questions.stem:
\(\frac{8(cx + 3)}{5} = 4x - 3\)

In the given equation, \(c\) is a constant. If the equation has no solution, what is the value of \(c\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Expand the left side to \(\frac{8c}{5}x + \frac{24}{5}\). A linear equation has no solution when the two sides have the same slope but different constants — parallel lines. Set \(\frac{8c}{5} = 4\), giving \(8c = 20\) and \(c = \frac{5}{2}\); the constants \(\frac{24}{5}\) and \(-3\) differ, so there really is no solution.

whyWrong.A: The sign is wrong, and matching slopes requires \(8c = 20\), a positive value.
whyWrong.B: This is the negative reciprocal-style slip; \(\frac{8c}{5} = 4\) does not give a negative \(c\).
whyWrong.C: This is the reciprocal of the answer — you solved \(\frac{8}{5}c = 4\) as \(c = \frac{4 \cdot 8}{5 \cdot 8}\) rather than \(c = \frac{4 \cdot 5}{8}\).

questions.stem: For what value of a is \( \sqrt[a]{r^{42}} \) equivalent to \( r^{6/7} \) , where r > 1 ?
questions.whyCorrect: Rewrite the radical as a power: \( \sqrt[a]{r^{42}} = r^{42/a} \) . Since the bases match and r > 1, the exponents must be equal: \( \frac{42}{a} = \frac{6}{7} \) . Cross-multiplying gives 6a = 294, so a = 49.

questions.stem:
(x − 2) − 8(y + 3) = 123
(x − 2) + 8(y + 3) = 432

The solution to the given system of equations is (x, y). What is the value of 10(x − 2)?
questions.whyCorrect: Do not expand. Treat (x − 2) and (y + 3) as single quantities: the second term is −8(y + 3) in one equation and +8(y + 3) in the other, so adding the equations cancels it and leaves 2(x − 2) = 123 + 432 = 555. Then x − 2 = 277.5, and the question asks for 10(x − 2), which is 2775.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by \( f(x) = 11x^{3} \). The graph of \( y = f(-x) + c \) in the xy-plane, where c is a positive integer constant, has an x-intercept at (r, 0) and a y-intercept at (0, t), where r and t are constants. Which of the following must be true about r and t?
questions.whyCorrect: Substitute before reasoning: \( f(-x) + c = 11(-x)^{3} + c = -11x^{3} + c \). At x = 0 the value is c, so t = c > 0. Setting \( -11r^{3} + c = 0 \) gives \( r^{3} = \frac{c}{11} \), which is positive, so r > 0 as well.

whyWrong.A: This is the graph of \( -11x^{3} \) with no upward shift — that curve passes through the origin, so it has neither a positive nor a negative intercept. Adding c moves both intercepts to the positive side.
whyWrong.B: r < 0 would require \( r^{3} \) to be negative, but \( r^{3} = \frac{c}{11} \) and c is positive.
whyWrong.D: t is found by putting x = 0 into \( -11x^{3} + c \), which leaves c, and c is stated to be a positive integer.

questions.stem:
For three counties, the table summarizes the number of residents who voted, by county and by candidate, during a 2016 US gubernatorial election. In 2016, the total number of residents in all three of these counties was 960,000, and the total area of these three counties was 1,949 square miles.

Candidate 1Candidate 2Other candidatesTotal
County A35,95434,7771,64072,371
County B165,97377,8376,862250,672
County C46,47554,2352,026102,736
Total248,402166,84910,528425,779

To the nearest whole percent, the total number of residents who voted for Candidate 1 is what percent of the total number of residents who voted for Candidate 2?
questions.whyCorrect: Use the two column totals, not one county's row: \(\frac{248{,}402}{166{,}849} \approx 1.4888\), which is about 149%. Candidate 1 got more votes than Candidate 2, so the answer must be above 100%.

whyWrong.A: This is the reciprocal, \(\frac{166{,}849}{248{,}402} \approx 67\%\) — Candidate 2 as a percent of Candidate 1. The question puts Candidate 1 on top.
whyWrong.B: This is County C's row alone, \(\frac{46{,}475}{54{,}235} \approx 86\%\). The question asks about the totals for all three counties.
whyWrong.C: This is County A's row alone, \(\frac{35{,}954}{34{,}777} \approx 103\%\), not the column totals.

questions.stem: Which quadratic equation has exactly one distinct real solution?
questions.whyCorrect: One distinct solution means a perfect square, or equivalently a discriminant of 0. Here \( x^{2} - 22x + 121 = (x - 11)^{2} \) , whose only solution is x = 11. Checking: \( (-22)^{2} - 4(1)(121) = 484 - 484 = 0 \) .

whyWrong.A: \( x^{2} = 22 \) has the two solutions \( \pm\sqrt{22} \) .
whyWrong.B: Factoring gives \( x(x - 11) = 0 \) , so x = 0 and x = 11, two solutions.
whyWrong.C: Its discriminant is \( 121 - 484 = -363 \) , which is negative, so it has no real solutions at all. Note how close it looks to D: the middle coefficient has to be 22 for the perfect square, since \( 2 \times 11 = 22 \) .

questions.stem: An environmental scientist needs to collect at least 38 samples of red clay soil for analysis. If \(r\) represents the number of samples the scientist collects for analysis, which inequality represents this situation?
questions.whyCorrect: “At least 38” means 38 is the smallest acceptable number, so \(r\) must be 38 or more: \(r\ge 38\).

whyWrong.A: This caps the count at 38 instead of requiring at least that many.
whyWrong.B: This says \(r\ge 76\) — the 38 has been subtracted for no reason.
whyWrong.C: This allows \(r\) to be far below 38, including 0.

questions.stem: Julia purchased 600 feet of fencing. She used 70% of this fencing to surround a vegetable garden. How many feet of fencing did Julia use to surround the vegetable garden?
questions.whyCorrect: 70% of 600 is 0.70 × 600 = 420 feet. Convert the percent to a decimal and multiply by the total; do not divide.

whyWrong.A: 14 is \(\frac{700}{50}\)-type arithmetic, or 600 divided by roughly 43; dividing by the percent instead of multiplying by it.
whyWrong.B: 35 is half of 70. You worked with the percent number itself rather than applying it to 600.
whyWrong.D: 530 is 600 − 70; you subtracted the percent as if it were a number of feet.

questions.stem: An agricultural scientist needs to collect at least 200 soil samples in a certain area for a study on soil quality. If the scientist has already collected 168 soil samples, what is the minimum number of additional soil samples the scientist needs to collect for the study?
questions.whyCorrect: The requirement is on the total, so subtract what is already collected from the target: 200 − 168 = 32. 'At least 200' includes exactly 200, so 32 more samples is enough.

whyWrong.A: 368 adds 200 and 168 instead of subtracting.
whyWrong.B: 12 comes from a borrowing slip in 200 − 168.
whyWrong.C: 148 comes from subtracting 20 rather than 200 − 168, or from mis-aligning the digits.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by \[ f(x) = 25x + 80. \] What is the value of \( f(x) \) when x = 2?
questions.whyCorrect: Substitute 2 for x: \( 25(2) + 80 = 50 + 80 = 130 \) . Only the x is replaced; the 80 is a constant and is added afterwards.

whyWrong.A: This is \( 25 \times 2 \) with the +80 left off.
whyWrong.B: This adds all three numbers, 25 + 80 + 2, instead of multiplying 25 by the input.
whyWrong.D: This multiplies the whole expression by 2, as if the input applied to the 80 as well.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((131y)^{\frac{1}{2}}\), where \(y > 1\)?
questions.whyCorrect: An exponent of \(\frac{1}{2}\) is a square root, and the exponent applies to everything inside the parentheses. So \((131y)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{131y}\).

whyWrong.A: Here the root was applied only to \(y\), leaving 131 outside untouched. The 131 is inside the parentheses, so it is under the root too.
whyWrong.B: This roots only the 131 and leaves \(y\) outside — the same mistake in reverse.
whyWrong.D: Squaring inside and then taking the root returns \(131y\) itself (for positive values), which is the original expression, not its square root.

questions.stem: The equation \(y = -4.9(x - 9.1)^2 + 10{,}700\) gives the estimated height above the ground, \(y\), in meters, of a plane, where \(x\) is the number of seconds since it started a parabolic maneuver. If this equation is graphed in the xy-plane, which of the following is the best interpretation of the vertex of the graph?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The plane reached an estimated maximum height of 10,700 meters 4.9 seconds after it started the parabolic maneuver.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The plane reached an estimated maximum height of 10,700 meters 9.1 seconds after it started the parabolic maneuver.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The plane reached an estimated maximum height of 4.9 meters 10,700 seconds after it started the parabolic maneuver.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The plane reached an estimated maximum height of 9.1 meters 10,700 seconds after it started the parabolic maneuver.

questions.whyCorrect: The equation is in vertex form \(y = a(x - h)^2 + k\), so the vertex is \((h, k) = (9.1,\ 10{,}700)\). Because \(a = -4.9\) is negative the parabola opens downward, so the vertex is a maximum. The \(x\)-coordinate is time and the \(y\)-coordinate is height, so the plane's greatest height, 10,700 meters, happens 9.1 seconds in.

whyWrong.A: 4.9 is the leading coefficient, not a coordinate of the vertex. It controls how fast the height falls away from the peak; it is not a time.
whyWrong.C: This swaps the roles of the two numbers and uses the leading coefficient as a height. The height at the vertex is the constant added at the end, 10,700.
whyWrong.D: This reads 9.1 as a height and 10,700 as a time. In \((x - 9.1)^2\) the 9.1 is subtracted from \(x\), which is time, so 9.1 is a number of seconds.

questions.note: Book prints the expression without 'y ='; restored, and the typos 'give'/'were'/'second' corrected.

questions.stem: Stefan purchased 500 feet of fencing. He used 80% of this fencing to surround a vegetable garden. How many feet of fencing did Stefan use to surround the vegetable garden?
questions.whyCorrect: Convert the percent to a decimal and multiply: 500 × 0.80 = 400 feet. The other 20%, or 100 feet, is what was left over.

whyWrong.A: This does not come from 500 and 80% by any correct step.
whyWrong.B: This is 500 − 80, treating the 80 as a count of feet instead of a percentage.
whyWrong.D: This is 8% of 500, from moving the decimal point one place too far when converting 80% to 0.80.

questions.stem: How many solutions does the equation 10x = 10 have?
questions.whyCorrect: Dividing both sides by 10 gives x = 1, a single value. A linear equation with a nonzero coefficient on x always has exactly one solution.

whyWrong.A: There would be no solution only if the x terms cancelled and left a false statement, like 0 = 1.
whyWrong.C: Two solutions require a squared term or an absolute value; this equation is linear.
whyWrong.D: Infinitely many solutions require both sides to be identical expressions, like 10x = 10x.

questions.stem:
\( P(t) = 1{,}200(1.06)^{t} \)
The function P gives the estimated number of sea lions in a certain area, where t is the number of years since a study began. What is the best interpretation of P(0) = 1,200 in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The estimated number of sea lions in the area increased by 1,200 each year during the study.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The estimated number of sea lions in the area increased by 106 each year during the study.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The estimated number of sea lions in the area was 1,200 when the study began.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The estimated number of sea lions in the area was 106 when the study began.

questions.whyCorrect: t counts years since the study began, so t = 0 is the moment the study began. P(0) is therefore the population at that moment, and the equation gives \( 1200(1.06)^{0} = 1200 \). Read P(0) as a starting value, not as a rate.

whyWrong.A: 1,200 is a population, not a yearly increase. The growth here is by a factor of 1.06 each year, which is 6 percent, not a fixed 1,200.
whyWrong.B: 106 does not appear in the function; 1.06 does, and it is a multiplier, not an amount added.
whyWrong.D: This confuses the base 1.06 with the starting value. P(0) is 1,200 by direct substitution.

questions.stem: What is 10% of 450?
questions.whyCorrect: Taking 10% of a number moves the decimal point one place to the left, so 10% of 450 is 45.

whyWrong.A: This is 45 − 10, subtracting the percent after taking it.
whyWrong.B: This is 450 − 10, treating the 10 as a quantity rather than a percentage.
whyWrong.C: This is 90% of 450, the amount left after removing 10%, not the 10% itself.

questions.stem: A right triangular pyramid has exactly six edges. Each of these edges is 96 centimeters long. If the surface area of the pyramid is \(k\sqrt{3}\) square centimeters, what is the value of k?
questions.whyCorrect: Six edges all of the same length means all four faces are congruent equilateral triangles — a regular tetrahedron, so the base counts as a face too. An equilateral triangle of side \(s\) has area \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^{2}\), so one face is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(96)^{2}=\frac{9216\sqrt{3}}{4}=2304\sqrt{3}\). Four of them give \(9216\sqrt{3}\), so k = 9216. The common slip is counting only the three slanted faces and getting 6,912.

questions.stem: A right rectangular prism has a base area of 28p square centimeters (cm<sup>2</sup>). The length of the base of the rectangular prism is 12 cm, and the height of the rectangular prism is 4 cm. Which expression represents the surface area, in cm<sup>2</sup>, of the right rectangular prism?
questions.whyCorrect: Get the width first: base area = length × width, so \(w=\frac{28p}{12}=\frac{7p}{3}\). Surface area is \(2(\ell w)+2(\ell h)+2(wh)\). The top and bottom give \(2(28p)=56p\); the two faces measuring 12 by 4 give \(2(48)=96\); the two faces measuring \(\frac{7p}{3}\) by 4 give \(2\cdot\frac{28p}{3}=\frac{56p}{3}\). Adding, \(56p+\frac{56p}{3}=\frac{168p+56p}{3}=\frac{224p}{3}\), so the total is \(\frac{224p}{3}+96\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(\frac{224p}{3}+96p\) collected into one fraction. The 96 comes from the two 12-by-4 faces, whose dimensions contain no p, so it must stay a constant.
whyWrong.C: This treats both pairs of side faces as 12 by 4, giving 4(48) = 192, which assumes the base is a square of side 12. Only one pair of side faces has the 12 cm edge; the other pair uses the width \(\frac{7p}{3}\).
whyWrong.D: The constant 96 is right but the p-term is far too big. It comes from multiplying by the base area 28p again rather than dividing it by the 12 cm length to find the width.

questions.stem:
Volume (cubic units)
Cylinder A\(72\pi\)
Cylinder B\(4{,}608\pi\)
The table shows the volume of two similar solids, right circular cylinder A and right circular cylinder B. The radius of right circular cylinder A is 3 units. The surface area of right circular cylinder A is \(k\pi\) square units, and the surface area of right circular cylinder B is \(n\pi\) square units, where k and n are constants. What is the value of \(n-k\)? (The surface area of a right circular cylinder with radius r and height h is \(2\pi r^{2}+2\pi rh\).)
questions.whyCorrect: Cylinder A first: \(\pi(3)^{2}h=72\pi\) gives h = 8, so its surface area is \(2\pi(9)+2\pi(3)(8)=18\pi+48\pi=66\pi\) and k = 66. For similar solids the volumes scale as the cube of the linear ratio, so \(\frac{4{,}608\pi}{72\pi}=64\) means the linear ratio is \(\sqrt[3]{64}=4\). Areas scale as the square of that ratio, \(4^{2}=16\), so \(n=16(66)=1{,}056\). Then \(n-k=1{,}056-66=990\). The step people miss is that the area ratio is 16, not 64.

questions.stem: \[x^{2}-6x+y^{2}-12y-36=0\]In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle. If this circle is inscribed in a square, what is the perimeter of the square?
questions.whyCorrect: Complete the square in both variables: \(x^{2}-6x\) needs +9 and \(y^{2}-12y\) needs +36, so the equation becomes \((x-3)^{2}+(y-6)^{2}=36+9+36=81\). The radius is \(\sqrt{81}=9\). A circle inscribed in a square touches all four sides, so the side of the square equals the diameter, 18. The perimeter is 4(18) = 72.

whyWrong.A: This is the side length of the square (the diameter of the circle), not the perimeter. Multiply by 4.
whyWrong.B: This is 4 times the radius. Each side of the square is the full diameter, 18, not the radius 9.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the correct perimeter, which happens if you take each side of the square to be twice the diameter instead of equal to it.

questions.stem: A circle in the xy-plane has a diameter with endpoints (a, 11) and (a, d), where a and d are constants. An equation of this circle is \((x-a)^{2}+(y-17)^{2}=r^{2}\), where r is a positive constant. What is the value of d?
questions.whyCorrect: The equation shows the center is (a, 17). The center of a circle is the midpoint of any diameter, so \(\frac{11+d}{2}=17\), giving \(11+d=34\) and d = 23. Equivalently, 17 is 6 above 11, so the other endpoint must be 6 above 17.

whyWrong.A: This goes 6 units the wrong way from 11. The center at 17 is above the endpoint at 11, so the other endpoint has to be above the center, not below the first endpoint.
whyWrong.B: This is the length of the diameter, 23 - 11 = 12, not the coordinate of the endpoint.
whyWrong.C: This is the y-coordinate of the center. The center lies between the two endpoints; it is not one of them.

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, a unit circle with center at the origin O contains point A with coordinates (1, 0) and point B with coordinates \(\left(\frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}, -\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\right)\). If the measure of angle AOB is p radians, what is the value of \(\frac{\cos p}{\sin p}\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Angle AOB is the angle at the origin between the ray toward (1, 0) and the ray toward B. Its measure is a positive number, so p is the size of that opening, \(p=\arctan\!\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)\), regardless of B sitting below the x-axis. Building the right triangle from B's coordinates, the leg along the x-axis is \(\frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}\) and the leg perpendicular to it is \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\) on a unit hypotenuse, so \(\cos p=\frac{5}{\sqrt{34}}\) and \(\sin p=\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\). The \(\sqrt{34}\) cancels in the quotient, leaving \(\frac{5}{3}\).
questions.note: Ambiguous as printed, and worth a human decision. Read strictly - 'the measure of angle AOB' is a geometric angle measure, so it is positive and sin p > 0 - the answer is 5/3. If the book instead intends B to be the terminal point of an angle in standard position, so that B = (cos p, sin p) with sin p negative, the answer is -5/3. I have recorded 5/3 because an angle measure cannot be negative, but the printed key is likely -5/3. Question 53 on the same page does not have this problem because its point B lies above the x-axis, where the two readings agree.

questions.stem: Point M lies on a unit circle in the xy-plane and has coordinates \((1, 0)\). Point C is the center of the circle at \((0, 0)\). Point N also lies on the unit circle, and the measure of angle MCN is \(\frac{385\pi}{6}\) radians. If the coordinates of point N are \((p, q)\), where p and q are constants, what is the value of q?
questions.whyCorrect: Strip off whole turns first. \(\frac{385\pi}{6} = \frac{384\pi}{6} + \frac{\pi}{6} = 64\pi + \frac{\pi}{6}\), and \(64\pi\) is 32 complete revolutions, so N sits where the angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) puts it. On the unit circle the coordinates are \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\), so \(q = \sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\) — it comes from rotating clockwise, or from subtracting the leftover \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) from a full turn instead of adding it.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) is \(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}\), which is p, the x-coordinate, not q.
whyWrong.C: This is the x-coordinate with a sign error: it uses cosine instead of sine and places the point in the wrong quadrant.

questions.note: The standard counterclockwise convention is assumed; a clockwise reading of the same angle would put N at -1/2.

questions.stem: \[2x^{2}+2y^{2}+tx+ty-78=0\]The given equation, where t is a positive constant, defines a circle in the xy-plane. The radius of this circle is \(\sqrt{41}\). What is the value of t?
questions.whyCorrect: Divide through by 2 first so the squared terms have coefficient 1: \(x^{2}+y^{2}+\frac{t}{2}x+\frac{t}{2}y-39=0\). Completing the square on each variable adds \(\left(\frac{t}{4}\right)^{2}\) twice, giving \(\left(x+\frac{t}{4}\right)^{2}+\left(y+\frac{t}{4}\right)^{2}=39+\frac{t^{2}}{8}\). Set that equal to \(r^{2}=41\): \(\frac{t^{2}}{8}=2\), so \(t^{2}=16\) and, since t is positive, t = 4. Skipping the division by 2 is the usual mistake - completing the square only works once the leading coefficients are 1.

questions.stem: The figure shows a rectangular pool surrounded by a concrete path that is x feet (ft) wide on all sides. The pool is 21 ft long and 13 ft wide. The area of the concrete path is 240 ft<sup>2</sup>. What is the value of x?
questions.whyCorrect: The path adds x to each of the four sides, so the outer rectangle is \((21+2x)\) by \((13+2x)\) - the width is added twice to each dimension, not once. The path is the outer rectangle minus the pool: \((21+2x)(13+2x)-21(13)=240\), so \((21+2x)(13+2x)=513\). Expanding gives \(4x^{2}+68x+273=513\), or \(x^{2}+17x-60=0\), which factors as \((x-3)(x+20)=0\). A width must be positive, so x = 3.

whyWrong.B: This is 2x, the total amount added to each dimension of the pool, not the width of the path itself.
whyWrong.C: This is the other root of the quadratic with its sign flipped. \(x=-20\) solves the equation algebraically but a path cannot have negative width, so it is rejected.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the rejected root, combining both errors above - the negative solution kept, then multiplied by 2.

questions.note: Figure needed: a shaded rectangle (the concrete path) with a smaller unshaded rectangle labelled 'Pool' centred inside it, and a vertical segment from the top of the outer rectangle to the top of the pool labelled 'x ft'. All dimensions are given in the stem, so the figure is illustrative.
questions.imageAlt: A shaded rectangle representing a concrete path, with a smaller white rectangle labelled Pool inside it; a short segment from the top of the outer rectangle to the top of the pool is labelled with the path width.

questions.stem: Two isosceles triangles are shown above. If 180 − z = 3y and y = 50, what is the value of x?
questions.whyCorrect: The angles of the right-hand triangle sum to 180, and its two tick-marked sides are congruent, so its two base angles are equal and together they measure \(180-z\). You are handed that quantity directly: \(180-z=3y=3(50)=150\), so each base angle is 75. The angle marked x is not that base angle - it sits on the other side of the slanted segment, between the segment and the upward continuation of the vertical line, so it is the base angle's supplement: \(x=180-75=105\). You never need z or the left-hand triangle at all.
questions.note: Figure needed, and the answer turns on one detail of it. Two vertical lines bound the figure. Four segments meet at a single point between them: two run left to the left-hand vertical line (marked with single ticks, forming the left isosceles triangle with apex angle y inside), two run right to the right-hand vertical line (marked with double ticks, forming the right isosceles triangle with apex angle z inside). The label x sits ABOVE the upper right-hand segment and to the LEFT of the right vertical line, i.e. in the wedge between that segment and the part of the vertical line running upward past the vertex - so x is the EXTERIOR angle there, 105, not the interior base angle, 75. If the printed key is 75, the disagreement is over exactly this label placement. Also note the four segments bend at the shared point (the upper-left segment does not continue as the lower-right one), so y and z are not vertical angles and there is no contradiction with y = 50.
questions.imageAlt: Two vertical lines with four segments meeting at a single point between them: two run left to the left-hand line and carry one tick mark each, two run right to the right-hand line and carry two tick marks each. Three angles are labelled with variables.

questions.stem: In the figure above, AB = AD, BC = CD, BE = 4, BC = 8, and AC = 12. What is the area of triangle ABD?
questions.whyCorrect: ABCD is a kite, so diagonal AC is the perpendicular bisector of BD: the diagonals meet at right angles at E and \(BD = 2(BE) = 8\). Right triangle BEC gives \(EC = \sqrt{8^2 - 4^2} = 4\sqrt{3}\), so the height from A is \(AE = AC - EC = 12 - 4\sqrt{3}\). Then the area of ABD is \(\frac{1}{2}(BD)(AE) = \frac{1}{2}(8)(12 - 4\sqrt{3}) = 48 - 16\sqrt{3}\).

whyWrong.A: This is \((BD)(AE)\) with the \(\frac{1}{2}\) of the triangle-area formula left out.
whyWrong.C: This uses \(BE = 4\) as the whole base instead of \(BD = 8\); E is the midpoint of BD, so the base is twice BE.
whyWrong.D: \(12 - 4\sqrt{3}\) is AE itself, the height of the triangle, not its area.

questions.note: Figure: kite ABCD with A at the left vertex, C at the right vertex, B above and D below; diagonals AC and BD cross at E.
questions.imageAlt: Line drawing of kite A B C D with A at the left, C at the right, B at the top and D at the bottom; the diagonals A C and B D are drawn and meet at point E.

questions.stem: The solid in the figure is the shaded part of a cone with a height of 10 cm obtained by cutting its top parallel to the base, 10 cm from its tip. The volume of the solid is
questions.whyCorrect: The shaded solid is a frustum: the whole cone (radius 3, height 20) with the small top cone (radius 1.5, height 10) removed. Work with the difference rather than memorising a frustum formula: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^{2}(20)-\frac{1}{3}\pi(1.5)^{2}(10)=60\pi-7.5\pi=52.5\pi\). That evaluates to about 164.93 cubic centimeters. The check that the setup is right is that the small cone is similar to the big one - half the radius and half the height.

whyWrong.A: \(60\pi\) is the volume of the entire cone, before the top is cut off. You still have to remove the small cone.
whyWrong.B: \(7.5\pi\) is the volume of the small cone that was cut away, not the piece that remains.
whyWrong.D: This is not produced by any correct route; it is close enough to the answer to look plausible. If you got it, check that you used the full cone's height of 20, not 10, and subtracted the small cone rather than averaging the two radii.

questions.note: Figure needed: a cone standing point-up, total height 20 marked on the right, the top 10 cm marked on the left, a horizontal cut 10 cm from the tip where the radius is 1.5, and a base radius of 3. The frustum below the cut is shaded. The radii 1.5 and 3 appear only in the figure, so the question is unanswerable without it.
questions.imageAlt: A cone standing point upward, cut by a horizontal plane parallel to the base; the piece below the cut is shaded. The height of the whole cone, the height of the removed tip, and the radius of both circles are marked with dimension lines.

questions.stem: A futuristic football is built from two right circular cones and a right circular cylinder with internal measurements represented by the figure above. Of the following, which is closest to the volume of the football, in cubic inches?
questions.whyCorrect: The solid is one cylinder plus two identical cones, all sharing the radius 3 in. The cylinder holds \(\pi(3)^2(6) = 54\pi\); each cone holds \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(3) = 9\pi\), so the two together add \(18\pi\). The total is \(72\pi \approx 226.2\) cubic inches.

whyWrong.A: \(18\pi \approx 56.5\) is the two cones alone, with the cylinder body left out.
whyWrong.B: \(54\pi \approx 169.6\) is the cylinder alone, with both pointed ends left out.
whyWrong.C: \(63\pi \approx 197.9\) counts the cylinder and only one cone; the football has a cone at each end.

questions.note: Figure: a vertical cylinder of height 6 in with a cone attached at each end; the label on the top face is a radius of 3 in, and each cone has height 3 in.
questions.imageAlt: Line drawing of a solid made of a vertical right circular cylinder with a right circular cone attached to each end; measurement bars label the height of the cylinder, the height of the upper cone and the radius of the top face.

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, a circle has center C with coordinates (p, 8), where p is a constant. Points G and H lie on the circle. Point G has coordinates \((p+3\sqrt{5},\, 14)\), and point H has coordinates (q, 8), where q is a constant greater than p. What is the area, in square units, of triangle CGH?
questions.whyCorrect: Find the radius from G: it sits \(3\sqrt{5}\) to the right of the center and 6 above it, so \(r=\sqrt{(3\sqrt{5})^{2}+6^{2}}=\sqrt{45+36}=\sqrt{81}=9\). The radical disappears, which is the whole point of the numbers chosen. H has the same y-coordinate as the center, so it is 9 units horizontally from C, and since q > p it is at \((p+9,\,8)\). Take CH as the base: it is horizontal with length 9, and G is 14 − 8 = 6 units above that line, so the area is \(\frac{1}{2}(9)(6)=27\).

whyWrong.A: This carries a stray \(\sqrt{5}\) from G's coordinate into the answer. Once you square \(3\sqrt{5}\) to get 45 and add 36, the radius is the whole number 9 and no radical survives.
whyWrong.C: \(5\sqrt{27}=15\sqrt{3}\approx 25.98\), which is close enough to 27 to look right but is not it. It comes from swapping the 5 and the 27 inside the radical rather than computing the base and height.
whyWrong.D: This attaches a \(\sqrt{6}\) to the correct value 27, taking the height 6 from under a radical it was never under. The height is exactly 6 units, the difference of the y-coordinates.

questions.stem: If \( 4x^{2} - 24x - 36 = 0 \) , what is the value of \( x^{2} - 6x \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Divide the whole equation by 4 first, so the quadratic and linear terms match what is asked for: \( x^{2} - 6x - 9 = 0 \) . Moving the constant across gives \( x^{2} - 6x = 9 \) . You never have to find x itself.

whyWrong.B: 6 is the coefficient in \( -6x \) copied out of the reduced equation, not a value of the expression.
whyWrong.C: 4 is the number you divided by, not the result. After dividing, the constant that moves across is \( \frac{36}{4} = 9 \) .
whyWrong.D: 0 treats the entire left side as \( x^{2} - 6x \) and forgets that the -9 has to be moved to the other side first.

questions.stem: One gallon of sealant costs $29 and will cover 300 square feet of a surface. A deck has a total surface area of \( d \) square feet. Which equation represents the cost \( c \), in dollars, of the sealant needed to cover the deck twice?
questions.whyCorrect: Covering twice means \( 2d \) square feet, so the gallons needed are \( \frac{2d}{300} = \frac{d}{150} \). Multiply by the $29 price per gallon: \( c = 29\left(\frac{d}{150}\right) \).

whyWrong.A: The price belongs in the numerator as a multiplier, not the denominator; this also uses one coat, not two.
whyWrong.B: Same inverted setup as A, with the 2 attached to the coverage figure instead of the area.
whyWrong.D: \( 29\left(\frac{d}{300}\right) \) covers the deck once and needs doubling.

questions.note: Same template as expressions-60 and expressions-84 (price per gallon differs only); flag the group at allocation.

questions.stem:
\( f(x) = 20(2)^{x} + 6(2)^{x} \)
The function f is defined by the given equation. Which of the following equivalent forms of f displays, as a coefficient or a base, the y-coordinate of the y-intercept of the graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane?
questions.whyCorrect: First find the y-intercept: \( f(0) = 20(1) + 6(1) = 26 \). Now you need the form in which 26 appears literally as a coefficient or a base. Combining the two like terms gives \( 26(2)^{x} \), which shows 26 outright.

whyWrong.A: This is equivalent, but the numbers on display are 80 and 24, neither of which is 26. You would still have to evaluate at x = 0 to find the intercept.
whyWrong.B: The displayed numbers here are 2, 10 and 3. The question asks for a form where the intercept value itself is visible without further work.
whyWrong.C: Rewriting base 2 as base 4 changes the base to 4 and leaves coefficients 20 and 6. Still no 26 on display.

questions.stem: \[ |15 - x| - 9 = 0 \]What are all positive solutions to the given equation?
questions.whyCorrect: Isolate the absolute value first: \( |15 - x| = 9 \). That splits into two equations, 15 − x = 9 and 15 − x = −9, giving x = 6 and x = 24. Both are positive, so both belong in the answer.

whyWrong.A: Both values are negative; substituting x = −6 gives \( |21| - 9 = 12 \), not 0.
whyWrong.B: −6 does not satisfy the equation, and the question asks only for positive solutions.
whyWrong.C: −24 does not satisfy the equation: \( |15 - (-24)| - 9 = 30 \).

questions.stem: Function f is defined as \( f(x) = (2x - 5)^{2} \) , and function g is defined as g(x) = 2(2x + 7). Which of the following is equivalent to f(x) + g(x) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Expand the square in full: \( (2x-5)^{2} = 4x^{2} - 20x + 25 \) - the middle term is \( 2 \cdot 2x \cdot (-5) \) , not just \( -25 \) . Then g(x) = 4x + 14. Adding gives \( 4x^{2} + (-20x + 4x) + (25 + 14) = 4x^{2} - 16x + 39 \) .

whyWrong.A: This subtracts the 14 from g instead of adding it: 25 − 14 = 11.
whyWrong.C: −6x comes from expanding the square as \( 4x^{2} - 10x + 25 \) , halving the correct middle term.
whyWrong.D: +24x comes from expanding \( (2x-5)^{2} \) with the wrong sign on the middle term, and the constant repeats the error in A.

questions.stem:
\[ 3x + 5y = 8 \]
\[ 9x + 15y = 24 \]For each real number \( r \), which of the following points lies on the graph of each equation in the \( xy \)-plane for the given system?
questions.whyCorrect: The second equation is exactly 3 times the first, so the two graphs are the same line and any point on \( 3x + 5y = 8 \) works. Solving that for \( x \) gives \( x = \frac{8 - 5y}{3} = -\frac{5y}{3} + \frac{8}{3} \), so with \( y = r \) the point is \( \left(-\frac{5r}{3} + \frac{8}{3},\ r\right) \). Substituting confirms it: \( 3\left(-\frac{5r}{3} + \frac{8}{3}\right) + 5r = -5r + 8 + 5r = 8 \).

whyWrong.A: This solves for \( x \) but then writes the result as the \( y \)-coordinate; substituting gives \( \frac{-16r + 40}{3} \), not 8.
whyWrong.B: Solving \( 3x + 5y = 8 \) for \( y \) gives \( -\frac{3r}{5} + \frac{8}{5} \); the sign on the \( r \) term is wrong here, and substituting gives \( 6r + 8 \).
whyWrong.D: Substituting gives \( -\frac{2r}{3} + 144 \), which equals 8 only for one particular \( r \), not for every real number.

questions.note: The book prints "For each real number, r which of the following"; the stray comma has been removed.

questions.stem: The function g is a quadratic function. In the xy-plane, the graph of \( y = g(x) \) has a vertex at (-1, -4) and passes through the points (-2, -43) and (1, -160). What is the value of \( g(0) - g(2) \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Start from vertex form, since the vertex is given: \( g(x) = a(x + 1)^{2} - 4 \) . Substituting (-2, -43) gives \( a(1) - 4 = -43 \) , so a = -39 (the point (1, -160) confirms it). Then \( g(0) = -39 - 4 = -43 \) and \( g(2) = -39(9) - 4 = -355 \) , so the difference is \( -43 - (-355) = 312 \) .

whyWrong.A: -121 comes from combining numbers copied out of the stem instead of evaluating g at 0 and at 2.
whyWrong.B: 0 is what you get from \( a(x - 1)^{2} - 4 \) , where the vertex sign is flipped: that function really does give the same value at x = 0 and x = 2. The vertex (-1, -4) makes the factor \( (x + 1) \) .
whyWrong.C: 117 is \( g(0) - g(1) = -43 - (-160) \) , which uses the given point at x = 1 instead of evaluating at x = 2.

questions.stem: Zuri has a goal to run at least 16 miles per week while training for a race. This week, she has run 4 miles. If \(x\) represents the additional number of miles Zuri needs to run this week to meet her goal, which inequality represents this situation?
questions.whyCorrect: Her weekly total is what she has already run plus the additional miles: \(4+x\). “At least 16” means that total must reach 16 or more, so \(4+x\ge 16\).

whyWrong.A: Subtracting \(x\) would mean the extra running reduces her total.
whyWrong.B: The total is right but \(\le\) would cap her mileage rather than set a floor.
whyWrong.C: Both errors: extra miles subtracted, and the comparison would then be impossible for positive \(x\).

questions.stem: \[x^{2}-16x+y^{2}-10y-55=0\]In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle. If this circle is inscribed in a square, what is the perimeter of the square?
questions.whyCorrect: Complete the square: \(x^{2}-16x\) needs +64 and \(y^{2}-10y\) needs +25, giving \((x-8)^{2}+(y-5)^{2}=55+64+25=144\). The radius is 12, so the diameter is 24. An inscribed circle touches all four sides of the square, so the square's side is that diameter, 24, and the perimeter is 4(24) = 96.

whyWrong.A: This is the side of the square (the diameter), not its perimeter.
whyWrong.B: This is 4 times the radius. The side of the square is the diameter 24, not the radius 12.
whyWrong.D: This is 4(55), using the constant term of the equation as though it were a length. That 55 has to be moved across and combined with the 64 and 25 from completing the square before you have \(r^{2}\).

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, a unit circle with center at the origin O contains point A with coordinates (1, 0) and point B with coordinates \(\left(-\frac{5}{\sqrt{89}}, \frac{8}{\sqrt{89}}\right)\). If the measure of angle AOB is w radians, what is the value of \(\tan w\)?
questions.whyCorrect: On a unit circle centered at the origin, a point reached by rotating the ray toward (1, 0) through w radians has coordinates \((\cos w, \sin w)\). Here B lies above the x-axis, so w is between 0 and \(\pi\) and the geometric angle AOB is exactly that rotation: \(\cos w=-\frac{5}{\sqrt{89}}\) and \(\sin w=\frac{8}{\sqrt{89}}\). Then \(\tan w=\frac{\sin w}{\cos w}=\frac{8/\sqrt{89}}{-5/\sqrt{89}}=-\frac{8}{5}\). Do not drop the sign - B is in the second quadrant, where tangent is negative.

questions.stem: If the perimeter of an equilateral triangle with a height of 21 is \( a\sqrt{3} \), what is the value of \(a\)?
questions.whyCorrect: The height of an equilateral triangle with side \(s\) splits it into two 30-60-90 triangles, giving \( h = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s \). So \( 21 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s \) and \( s = \frac{42}{\sqrt{3}} = 14\sqrt{3} \). The perimeter is \( 3s = 42\sqrt{3} \), so \( a = 42 \).

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
In the figure, \(\angle ABD = w^\circ\), \(\angle CAD = z^\circ\), and \(\cos w = \frac{9}{41}\). What is the value of \(\tan z\)?
questions.whyCorrect: The altitude from the right angle splits the triangle into two triangles similar to the original, and the quick consequence is \(z = w\): in right triangle ABD, \(\angle BAD = 90^\circ - w\), and since \(\angle BAC = 90^\circ\), \(z = 90^\circ - \angle BAD = w\). From \(\cos w = \frac{9}{41}\), the triangle is a 9-40-41 right triangle, so \(\sin w = \frac{40}{41}\) and \(\tan z = \tan w = \frac{40}{9}\).
