questions.stem: In the xy-plane, the line y = 3x − 14 is tangent to a circle with center (h, 1). Which of the following is a possible value for h if the center lies to the right of the tangent line?
questions.whyCorrect: The radius is never given, so tangency alone puts no restriction on h - any center can be tangent to the line for the right radius. The only condition that bites is the position. Find where the line reaches the height of the center: set y = 1, so 1 = 3h − 14 gives x = 5. At the height y = 1 the line sits at x = 5, so the center (h, 1) is to the right of the line exactly when h > 5. Only 7 qualifies.

whyWrong.A: 2 is less than 5, so this center sits to the left of the line.
whyWrong.B: 3 is less than 5, so this center also sits to the left of the line.
whyWrong.C: At h = 5 the point (5, 1) lies exactly on the line y = 3x − 14, not to the right of it, and a center on the tangent line is impossible anyway.

questions.stem: Identical rectangles X and Y each have an area of \(\frac{49}{5}\) square meters and a perimeter of P meters. If one of the shorter sides of rectangle X is glued to one of the shorter sides of rectangle Y, the resulting rectangle has a perimeter of \(\frac{14}{9}P\) meters. What is the value of P?
questions.whyCorrect: Call the long side L and the short side s, so \(P = 2(L+s)\). Gluing along the short sides makes a \(2L \times s\) rectangle of perimeter \(4L + 2s\), so \(4L + 2s = \frac{14}{9}(2L+2s)\), which simplifies to \(8L = 10s\), i.e. \(L = \frac{5}{4}s\). Substituting into \(Ls = \frac{49}{5}\) gives \(s^2 = \frac{196}{25}\), so \(s = \frac{14}{5}\) and \(L = \frac{7}{2}\), and \(P = 2\left(\frac{7}{2} + \frac{14}{5}\right) = 12.6\).

questions.stem: In the figure above, P and N are the centers of the circles and PN = 6. What is the area of the intersection?
questions.whyCorrect: Each circle passes through the other's center, so both radii equal \(PN = 6\). The common chord subtends a \(120^\circ\) angle at each center, so one circular segment is sector minus triangle: \(\frac{1}{2}(6)^2\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) - \frac{1}{2}(6)^2\sin 120^\circ = 12\pi - 9\sqrt{3}\). The lens is two such segments, one from each circle: \(24\pi - 18\sqrt{3}\).

whyWrong.A: This uses a half circle, \(18\pi\), in place of the \(120^\circ\) sector and then counts only one segment.
whyWrong.B: This doubles the sector correctly but subtracts the triangle only once; each of the two segments has its own triangle to remove.
whyWrong.D: \(36\pi\) is the area of an entire circle, not two \(120^\circ\) sectors; only a third of each circle lies on the sector side of the chord.

questions.note: Figure: two congruent overlapping circles with centres P (left) and N (right), each passing through the other's centre; the shaded lens is their overlap and PN is drawn across it.
questions.imageAlt: Line drawing of two overlapping circles of equal size with centres P and N marked and joined by a segment; the lens-shaped region where the circles overlap is shaded.

questions.stem: In a circle, chord RS is parallel to diameter PQ. If the length of RS is \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the length of PQ and the distance between the chord and the diameter is \(2\sqrt{7}\), what is the radius of the circle?
questions.whyCorrect: Write everything in terms of the radius r. The diameter is 2r, so \(RS=\frac{3}{4}(2r)=\frac{3r}{2}\) and half the chord is \(\frac{3r}{4}\). Drop the perpendicular from the center to the chord: it has length \(2\sqrt{7}\) and, with half the chord, forms a right triangle whose hypotenuse is a radius. So \(r^{2}=\left(\frac{3r}{4}\right)^{2}+(2\sqrt{7})^{2}=\frac{9r^{2}}{16}+28\). Then \(\frac{7r^{2}}{16}=28\), \(r^{2}=64\), r = 8. The trap is using \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the radius, or forgetting to halve the chord.

whyWrong.A: 6 is half of the chord RS once you know r = 8 (RS = 12), an intermediate value rather than the radius.
whyWrong.B: This scales the given distance \(2\sqrt{7}\) by \(\frac{3}{2}\). The chord ratio does not act on the distance; the distance and half the chord are the two legs of a right triangle, so they combine by the Pythagorean theorem, not by multiplication.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the given distance, treating \(2\sqrt{7}\) as half the radius. The perpendicular distance is a leg of the right triangle, not a piece of the radius.

questions.stem:
In the figure shown, \( AB = \sqrt{89} \) units, AC = 8 units, and CE = 24 units. What is the area, in square units, of triangle ADE?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.whyCorrect: Get BC from the small right triangle: \( BC = \sqrt{89 - 64} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \) . Triangles ABC and ADE share angle A and both have a right angle, so they are similar, and the scale factor is \( \frac{AE}{AC} = \frac{8 + 24}{8} = 4 \) . So DE = 4(5) = 20 and the area of ADE is \( \frac{1}{2}(32)(20) = 320 \) . The trap is using AC = 8 as the base of the big triangle; its base is the whole of AE = 32.
questions.note: Measured reading of the figure: A, C and E lie on one horizontal line in that order; B is directly above C with a right angle marked at C, and D is directly above E with a right angle marked at E; A, B and D are collinear, so ABC and ADE are nested similar right triangles sharing the vertex A.
questions.imageAlt: A plane diagram of two nested right triangles sharing a common vertex: a horizontal base line with two labelled points on it, two vertical segments rising from those points with their right angles marked, and a slanted line through the tops of both.

questions.stem: If \( 4x^{2} - 12x - 24 = 0 \) , what is the value of \( x^{2} - 3x \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Divide the whole equation by 4 so the first two terms match the expression asked about: \( x^{2} - 3x - 6 = 0 \) . Moving the constant across gives \( x^{2} - 3x = 6 \) . Solving for x is never necessary.

whyWrong.A: 0 treats the entire left side as \( x^{2} - 3x \) , leaving the -6 behind.
whyWrong.B: 3 is the coefficient in \( -3x \) , a number copied from the expression rather than its value.
whyWrong.C: 4 is the factor you divided by. After dividing, the constant that crosses over is \( \frac{24}{4} = 6 \) .

questions.stem: A machine makes 9-inch, 8-inch, and 3-inch parts. During a certain day, the number of 9-inch parts that the machine makes is 4 times the number \( n \) of 8-inch parts, and the number of 3-inch parts is 15. During this day, the machine makes 100 parts in total. Which equation represents this situation?
questions.whyCorrect: The 100 counts parts, not inches, so the lengths 9, 8 and 3 never enter the equation — they only name the three kinds of part. The counts are \( 4n \) nine-inch parts, \( n \) eight-inch parts and 15 three-inch parts, so \( 4n + n + 15 = 100 \), which simplifies to 5n + 15 = 100.

whyWrong.A: This multiplies each count by its length, so the left side is a total length in inches while the right side is a count of parts.
whyWrong.B: This also weights by length and, worse, uses \( n \) for all three counts, ignoring both the "4 times" relationship and the 15.
whyWrong.C: This counts the 9-inch parts but drops the \( n \) eight-inch parts entirely.

questions.note: Same template as expressions-93 (lengths and multiplier changed); flag as a near-duplicate pair at allocation.

questions.stem: The number of bacteria in a growth medium is expected to increase by 160% every 2 hours during a period of observation. The number of bacteria in the growth medium was estimated to be 8,000 when the period of observation began. Which function P gives the expected number of bacteria in this growth medium t hours after the period of observation began?
questions.whyCorrect: Two decisions here. An increase of 160% means the new amount is the old amount plus 160% of it, so the multiplier is 1 + 1.60 = 2.60, not 1.60. And the multiplier applies once every 2 hours, so in t hours it applies \( \frac{t}{2} \) times — divide by 2, do not multiply.

whyWrong.A: 1.60 would be a 60% increase. "Increase by 160%" means the amount ends up at 260% of what it was.
whyWrong.B: Both parts are wrong: 1.60 is the wrong multiplier and the exponent 2t makes the growth happen twice per hour instead of once per two hours.
whyWrong.D: The multiplier 2.60 is right, but 2t counts four doublings-worth of growth in the time only one should occur. Check it at t = 2: this gives \( 2.60^{4} \), not \( 2.60^{1} \).

questions.stem: The equation \(4|x - 3| = k\) , where \(k\) is a constant, has exactly one solution. Which of the following could be the value of \(\frac{k}{4}\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Divide both sides by 4 first: \(|x - 3| = \frac{k}{4}\). An absolute value equal to a positive number has two solutions, equal to a negative number has none, and equal to 0 has exactly one. So \(\frac{k}{4}\) must be 0.

whyWrong.A: A negative right side gives no solutions, since an absolute value is never negative.
whyWrong.B: \(-3\) gives no solutions and \(3\) gives two; neither gives exactly one.
whyWrong.D: \(|x-3| = 3\) has the two solutions \(x = 6\) and \(x = 0\), not one. The 3 inside the bars is a distractor.

questions.stem: The function is defined by \( f(x) = \frac{x + 11}{5} \) , and f(a) = −18, where a is a constant. What is the value of a?
questions.whyCorrect: Set the formula equal to the output: \( \frac{a + 11}{5} = -18 \) . Multiply both sides by 5 first, giving a + 11 = −90, then subtract 11 to get a = −101. Multiplying before subtracting is the order that matters here.

whyWrong.B: −79 comes from subtracting 11 before multiplying by 5, i.e. treating the equation as a + 11 = −90 − 11 reversed.
whyWrong.C: \( -\frac{79}{5} \) divides by 5 instead of multiplying by it.
whyWrong.D: \( -\frac{7}{5} \) comes from subtracting 11 from −18 and then dividing, doing both operations backwards.

questions.stem:
y = 5x + 7
y = −4x − 11

The solution to the given system of equations is (x, y). What is the value of y?
questions.whyCorrect: Both equations are already solved for y, so set the right sides equal: 5x + 7 = −4x − 11. Add 4x to both sides and subtract 7: 9x = −18, so x = −2. The question asks for y, so go one step further: y = 5(−2) + 7 = −3, and the other equation checks out at −4(−2) − 11 = −3.

whyWrong.A: This is 9x, the value you get just before dividing by 9. Finish the division to get x = −2, then substitute to find y.
whyWrong.B: This is the coefficient −4 from the second equation, not a coordinate of the solution. Neither x nor y equals −4 here.
whyWrong.D: This is x, not y. The question asks for the y-coordinate, so substitute x = −2 back into either equation to get y = −3.

questions.stem:
For the quadratic function f, the table shows three values of x and their corresponding values of \( f(x) \) .
xf(x)
-14
012
122
Which equation defines f?
questions.whyCorrect: Every choice already has the right constant, since \( f(0) = 12 \) . So test the other two rows. At x = 1 the sum \( a + b + 12 \) must be 22, so \( a + b = 10 \) ; at x = -1 the value \( a - b + 12 \) must be 4, so \( a - b = -8 \) . Solving the pair gives a = 1 and b = 9.

whyWrong.A: It gives 22 at x = 1, but at x = -1 it gives \( 5 - 5 + 12 = 12 \) , not 4. Checking only one row is what lets this one through.
whyWrong.B: It also gives 22 at x = 1, but at x = -1 it gives \( 9 - 1 + 12 = 20 \) .
whyWrong.C: At x = 1 it gives \( 9 - 1 + 12 = 20 \) , so it fails the row it was probably built to satisfy.

questions.stem: The walls of a small apartment were covered using exactly 3 gallons of paint. The paint was spread uniformly over a total area of 960 square feet. What was the rate, in gallons per square foot, at which the paint was used?
questions.whyCorrect: The units tell you the fraction: gallons per square foot means gallons on top, square feet on the bottom. That is \(\frac{3 \text{ gallons}}{960 \text{ square feet}} = \frac{1}{320}\) gallon per square foot.

whyWrong.A: This is 1 gallon over 960 square feet, forgetting that 3 gallons were used.
whyWrong.C: This is \(\frac{960}{3}\), which is square feet per gallon — the reciprocal rate, in the other unit.
whyWrong.D: This is the total area, not a rate at all.

questions.stem: A machine makes 8-inch, 5-inch, and 7-inch parts. During a certain day, the number of 8-inch parts that the machine makes is 3 times the number \( n \) of 5-inch parts, and the number of 7-inch parts is 12. During this day, the machine makes 100 parts total. Which equation represents this situation?
questions.whyCorrect: The total of 100 is a count of parts, so the part lengths play no role in the equation. There are \( 3n \) eight-inch parts, \( n \) five-inch parts and 12 seven-inch parts, giving \( 3n + n + 12 = 100 \), i.e. 4n + 12 = 100.

whyWrong.A: Multiplying each count by its length gives a total in inches, which cannot equal a number of parts.
whyWrong.B: This weights by length and uses \( n \) for every category, throwing away both the "3 times" relationship and the 12.
whyWrong.C: This counts only the 8-inch parts and the 7-inch parts, leaving out the \( n \) five-inch parts.

questions.note: Same template as expressions-91; flag as a near-duplicate pair at allocation.

questions.stem:
\(f(x)=4\big(g(x)\big)-2\)
\(g(x)=|13x-8|\)
The functions \(f\) and \(g\) are defined by the given equations. What is the value of \(f(-10)\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Work from the inside out. \(g(-10)=|13(-10)-8|=|-138|=138\) — the absolute value makes it positive. Then \(f(-10)=4(138)-2=552-2=550\).

whyWrong.A: −554 comes from skipping the absolute value and using \(-138\).
whyWrong.B: −42 treats \(f\) as \(4x-2\), substituting −10 directly instead of \(g(-10)\).
whyWrong.D: 138 is \(g(-10)\); the outer function still has to be applied.

questions.stem: To win a game show, a contestant needs to score at least 70 total points from two rounds. Correct responses in the first round are worth 4 points each, and correct responses in the second round are worth 5 points each. Which inequality models this situation, where \(f\) is the number of correct responses in the first round and \(s\) is the number of correct responses in the second round?
questions.whyCorrect: Points earned are \(4f\) in the first round and \(5s\) in the second. “At least 70” means the total can equal 70 or exceed it, so the symbol is \(\ge\): \(4f+5s\ge 70\).

whyWrong.A: This counts responses rather than points and points the inequality the wrong way.
whyWrong.C: The point values are attached to the wrong rounds, and the second round loses its 5.
whyWrong.D: Both the point values are swapped and the direction is wrong — scoring more than 70 still wins.

questions.stem: The ratio 6 to 3 is equivalent to the ratio 24 to 3k, where k is a constant. What is the value of k ?
questions.whyCorrect: Write the two ratios as a proportion: \( \frac{6}{3} = \frac{24}{3k} \) . The left side is 2, so \( 3k = \frac{24}{2} = 12 \) . Dividing by 3 gives k = 4 — the last step is the one people skip, because the unknown is 3k, not k.

whyWrong.A: This is \( \frac{3}{4} \) , from inverting the proportion — you divided the wrong pair.
whyWrong.C: This is 3k, the value you find on the way. Divide it by 3 to get k.
whyWrong.D: This is \( 24 \times 3 \) , from cross-multiplying only part of the proportion.

questions.stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=10x^2-38x-150\). What is the value of \(f(0)\) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Substitute 0 for \(x\): the \(x^2\) and \(x\) terms both become 0, leaving \(f(0)=-150\). Evaluating any polynomial at 0 always returns its constant term.

whyWrong.B: \(-38\) is the coefficient of \(x\); that term is multiplied by 0 and disappears.
whyWrong.C: 0 is the input, not the output. The constant term keeps the output away from 0.
whyWrong.D: 10 is the coefficient of \(x^2\), which is also multiplied by 0.

questions.stem: In the figure, \(\overline{AC}\) is a diameter of the circle with centre \(O\), and \(AC = 10\). Triangle \(ACB\) is equilateral, and \(P\) is the point where \(\overline{BO}\) crosses the circle. The length of \(\overline{BP}\) is \(n\) times the length of \(\overline{AO}\). What is the value of \(n\)?
questions.whyCorrect: The radius is \(AO = 5\). In the equilateral triangle with side 10, the segment from \(B\) to the midpoint \(O\) of \(\overline{AC}\) is the altitude, so \(BO = \frac{10\sqrt{3}}{2} = 5\sqrt{3}\). \(P\) sits on that segment where it meets the circle, so \(OP\) is a radius, 5. Then \(BP = BO - OP = 5\sqrt{3} - 5 = 5(\sqrt{3} - 1)\), which is \((\sqrt{3} - 1)\) times \(AO = 5\).

whyWrong.A: \(\sqrt{5}\) does not arise here; the equilateral triangle brings in \(\sqrt{3}\), not \(\sqrt{5}\).
whyWrong.B: \(\sqrt{3}\) is the ratio \(\frac{BO}{AO}\) — the whole altitude, before subtracting the radius \(OP\) to get down to \(BP\).
whyWrong.D: Right shape, wrong radical: this would follow from an altitude of \(5\sqrt{5}\), which no equilateral triangle has.

questions.note: The book defines P only in the figure; the stem now states that P is where BO crosses the circle so the question stands without the picture.

questions.stem: In the figure, \(RT = TU\), the measure of angle \(VST\) is 23° and the measure of angle \(RVS\) is 44°. What is the value of \(x\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Work in triangle \(USV\) first. Because \(T\) lies on segment \(US\), angle \(VST\) and angle \(VSU\) are the same angle, so the angle at \(S\) is 23°. Because \(U\), \(V\), \(R\) are collinear, angle \(UVS\) = 180° − 44° = 136°. That leaves angle \(SUV\) = 180 − 136 − 23 = 21°. Now use \(RT = TU\): triangle \(RTU\) is isosceles, so its base angles at \(U\) and \(R\) are both 21°, and \(x = 180 - 21 - 21 = 138\).
questions.note: Needs the figure. Reading of the page image: U, V, R lie on one horizontal line in that order; S is above and right of R; segment US passes through T; segment TR runs from T down to R and crosses segment VS; x° marks the angle at T between ray TU and ray TR, inside triangle RTU. Labelled "Figure not drawn to scale" is not printed for this item.

questions.stem:
The side lengths of triangle \(RST\) are given.
\(RS = 504\)
\(ST = 128\)
\(TR = 520\)
Triangle \(RST\) is similar to triangle \(UVW\), where \(S\) corresponds to \(V\) and \(T\) corresponds to \(W\). What is the value of \(\tan W\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles, so \(\tan W = \tan T\) and you can work entirely inside \(RST\). Check the side lengths: \(128^{2} + 504^{2} = 270{,}400 = 520^{2}\), so the triangle is right-angled at \(S\), with \(TR\) the hypotenuse. For angle \(T\), the opposite leg is \(RS = 504\) and the adjacent leg is \(ST = 128\), so \(\tan T = \frac{504}{128} = \frac{63}{16}\).

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{16}{65}\) is \(\cos T\) reduced (\(\frac{128}{520}\)), not the tangent.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{16}{63}\) inverts the ratio — it is \(\tan R\), the tangent of the other acute angle.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{63}{65}\) is \(\sin T\) (\(\frac{504}{520}\)); tangent uses the two legs, not a leg and the hypotenuse.

questions.stem: The product of a positive number \(x\) and the number that is 7 less than \(x\) is equal to 228. What is the value of \(x\)?
questions.whyCorrect: "The number that is 7 less than \(x\)" is \(x - 7\), so the sentence says \(x(x - 7) = 228\). Expand and set to zero: \(x^2 - 7x - 228 = 0\). Look for two numbers with product \(-228\) and sum \(-7\): those are \(-19\) and 12, so \((x - 19)(x + 12) = 0\). Only \(x = 19\) is positive.

questions.stem: If \(\frac{2a}{b} = 6.5\) and \(\frac{a}{bn} = 26\), what is the value of \(n\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Halve the first equation to get \(\frac{a}{b} = 3.25\). The second is \(\frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{1}{n} = 26\), so \(\frac{3.25}{n} = 26\) and \(n = \frac{3.25}{26} = 0.125 = \frac{1}{8}\). Watch the two traps: halve 6.5 first, and the question asks for \(n\), not \(\frac{1}{n}\) (which is 8).
questions.note: Free-response answer is 1/8; the equivalent decimal .125 should also be accepted.

questions.stem: The population of a certain city doubled every 75 years from 1657 to 1957. The population of this city was 240,000 in 1957. What was the population of this city in 1657?
questions.whyCorrect: Count the doublings first: 1957 - 1657 = 300 years, and 300 divided by 75 is 4, so the population doubled 4 times. Doubling four times multiplies by \( 2^{4} = 16 \). Working backwards, the 1657 population is \( \frac{240{,}000}{16} = 15{,}000 \).

questions.stem:
\(\frac{1}{6}(x + 2) - \frac{1}{5}(x + 2) = -5\)

What value of \(x\) is the solution to the given equation?
questions.whyCorrect: Both terms share the factor \(x + 2\), so combine the coefficients instead of expanding: \(\frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{5} = -\frac{1}{30}\). That gives \(-\frac{x+2}{30} = -5\), so \(x + 2 = 150\) and \(x = 148\).

whyWrong.A: There is no step producing \(-7\); the combined coefficient is small and negative, so \(x + 2\) has to be large and positive.
whyWrong.B: This makes the left side 0, not \(-5\). It is the value that kills the common factor.
whyWrong.D: This comes from combining the two fractions over the wrong common denominator. Substituting 270 makes the left side \(-\frac{272}{30}\), which is about \(-9.07\), not \(-5\).

questions.stem:
\( f(x) = 5(g(x)) - 3 \)
\( g(x) = |13x - 9| \)
The functions f and g are defined by the given equations. What is the value of \( f(-10) \)?
questions.whyCorrect: Work from the inside out. First \( g(-10) = |13(-10) - 9| = |-139| = 139 \) — the absolute value makes it positive. Then \( f(-10) = 5(139) - 3 = 695 - 3 = 692 \).

whyWrong.B: 139 is g(-10), the inner value. You still have to put it through f: multiply by 5 and subtract 3.
whyWrong.C: 698 comes from adding 3 instead of subtracting it: 695 + 3. The definition of f subtracts 3.
whyWrong.D: -53 is 5(-10) - 3, which applies f directly to -10 instead of to g(-10). The input to f here is the output of g, which is 139.

questions.stem:
y = 6x + 16
−7x − y = 36

What is the solution (x, y) to the given system of equations?
questions.whyCorrect: The first equation is already solved for y, so substitute it into the second and keep the parentheses: −7x − (6x + 16) = 36. The minus sign applies to both terms, giving −7x − 6x − 16 = 36, so −13x = 52 and x = −4. Then y = 6(−4) + 16 = −8.

whyWrong.B: The x-value \(-\frac{20}{13}\) comes from forgetting to distribute the minus sign onto the 16, which turns 36 + 16 = 52 into 36 − 16 = 20. Keep the parentheses and you get −13x = 52 instead.
whyWrong.C: The sign on x is lost: 13x = 52 gives 4, but the equation is −13x = 52, so x = −4. Checking (4, 40) in the second equation gives −28 − 40 = −68, not 36.
whyWrong.D: The point does satisfy y = 6x + 16, so it looks plausible, but a solution has to satisfy both equations. Substituting into the second gives −7(20) − 136 = −276, not 36.

questions.stem: The graph of the quadratic function \(y = f(x)\) in the xy-plane intersects the x-axis when \(x = 39\) and when \(x = p\), where \(p\) is a constant. The maximum value of \(y = f(x)\) occurs at the point \((14, m)\), where \(m\) is a constant. What is the value of \(p\)?
questions.whyCorrect: The maximum occurs at the vertex, and a parabola's vertex is exactly halfway between its two x-intercepts. So \(\frac{39 + p}{2} = 14\), which gives \(39 + p = 28\) and \(p = -11\). The value of \(m\) is never needed.

questions.stem: A certain hybrid car uses 39 gallons of gasoline to travel 1,950 miles. At this rate, how many kilometers does the car travel using 39 gallons of gasoline? (Use 1 mile = 1.6 kilometers.)
questions.whyCorrect: The gallons are the same in both statements, so nothing has to be scaled — only the units change. Convert 1,950 miles: \(1{,}950 \times 1.6 = 3{,}120\) kilometers.

whyWrong.A: This is off by a factor of ten, e.g. from \(1{,}950 \times 0.16\).
whyWrong.C: This is ten times too large; check that \(1{,}950 \times 1.6\) is a little over 3,000, not over 30,000.
whyWrong.D: This is a hundred times too large. It also comes from dividing the 1,950 miles by the 39 gallons and then mis-scaling, but the question already fixes the fuel at 39 gallons.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((3x^{3} - 8x + 5) - (4x^{6} + 9x - 2)\)?
questions.whyCorrect: The minus sign in front of the second parentheses flips the sign of all three terms inside it: \(-4x^{6} - 9x + 2\). Now collect like terms: \(-4x^{6}\) stands alone, \(3x^{3}\) stands alone, \(-8x - 9x = -17x\), and \(5 + 2 = 7\). The result is \(-4x^{6}+3x^{3}-17x+7\).

whyWrong.B: This combines \(3x^{3}\) and \(4x^{6}\) into a single \(x^{9}\) term by adding exponents. Exponents add when powers are multiplied, not when terms are subtracted. The constant sign is wrong too.
whyWrong.C: Same invented \(x^{9}\) term, plus subtracting 8x from 9x in the wrong order and mishandling the constants.
whyWrong.D: This distributes the minus only to the first term inside the parentheses: \(9x\) and \(-2\) keep their original signs, giving \(+x\) and \(+3\) instead of \(-17x\) and \(+7\).

questions.stem: The function f is defined by \( f(x) = 8 + \sqrt{x} \) . What is the value of \( f(36) \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Substitute 36 for x. The square root of 36 is 6, so \( f(36) = 8 + 6 = 14 \) . The 8 is added after the root is taken, not inside it.

whyWrong.A: 0 would require \( \sqrt{36} = -8 \) . You may have set the output equal to 0 and tried to solve instead of substituting the input.
whyWrong.C: 17 is 8 + 9, which treats the square root of 36 as 9. 9 is the square root of 81; \( 6^2 = 36 \) .
whyWrong.D: 26 is 8 + 18, which halves 36 instead of taking its square root.

questions.stem: An object travels x inches in y seconds. At this rate, which expression represents the time, in seconds, it takes the object to travel a distance of 22x inches?
questions.whyCorrect: The distance has been multiplied by 22 and the speed has not changed, so the time is multiplied by 22 as well. If x inches takes y seconds, 22x inches takes 22y seconds. Set up the proportion \( \frac{x}{y} = \frac{22x}{t} \) and it gives t = 22y.

whyWrong.A: This divides 22 by the time, which is neither a time nor dimensionally sensible. More distance at the same speed means more time, not less.
whyWrong.B: Dividing by 22 makes the trip 22 times faster. The object is travelling 22 times as far, so it takes longer.
whyWrong.D: Adding 22 treats the multiplier as a fixed number of extra seconds. The relationship is proportional, so the multiplier scales the time.

questions.stem: If 6x + 36 = 54, what is the value of x + 6?
questions.whyCorrect: Divide the whole equation by 6 in one step: \(x + 6 = 9\). (Or solve normally: \(6x = 18\), \(x = 3\), so \(x + 6 = 9\).)

whyWrong.A: 6 is the constant being added, not the value of the expression.
whyWrong.C: 36 is the constant in the original equation, before dividing by 6.
whyWrong.D: This is \(36 + 6\); the 36 has to be divided by 6 along with everything else.

questions.stem: If \( (x + 3)^{2} = 30 \) , what is the value of \( x^{2} + 6x \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Expand the square instead of solving for x: \( (x + 3)^{2} = x^{2} + 6x + 9 \) , so \( x^{2} + 6x + 9 = 30 \) and \( x^{2} + 6x = 21 \) . You never need the two irrational values of x.

whyWrong.B: 30 forgets that the expansion carries an extra +9, which has to come off the other side.
whyWrong.C: 39 adds 9 to 30 instead of subtracting it. The 9 is on the same side as \( x^{2} + 6x \) , so it moves across as -9.
whyWrong.D: 60 doubles 30, which would follow from squaring or doubling the equation rather than expanding the left side.

questions.stem: A certain goose species can fly at an average speed of 16 meters per second when in continuous flight. At this rate, how many meters would this goose species fly in 6 seconds?
questions.whyCorrect: A speed in meters per second multiplied by a time in seconds gives a distance in meters: 16 × 6 = 96 meters. Checking the units is what tells you to multiply rather than add or subtract.

whyWrong.B: This is the speed itself, the distance covered in one second, not in six.
whyWrong.C: This is 16 − 6. Subtracting a time from a speed is not a legal operation — the units do not match.
whyWrong.D: This is 16 + 6, adding a speed to a time. Again the units show the operation is wrong.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((5a^{2} - 3ab + 7b^{2}) - (4a^{2} + ab - 2b^{2})\)?
questions.whyCorrect: The minus sign applies to every term in the second bracket: \(-4a^{2} - ab + 2b^{2}\). Now combine like terms: \(5a^{2}-4a^{2}=a^{2}\), \(-3ab-ab=-4ab\), \(7b^{2}+2b^{2}=9b^{2}\).

whyWrong.B: Here the minus was distributed only onto the first term. Subtracting \(+ab\) gives \(-4ab\), and subtracting \(-2b^{2}\) gives \(+9b^{2}\).
whyWrong.C: Adding and subtracting like terms never changes the exponents; \(a^{2}\) stays \(a^{2}\), it does not become \(a^{4}\).
whyWrong.D: Both errors at once: the exponents were doubled and the subtraction was not distributed across the whole bracket.

questions.stem:
\( P(t) = 1{,}900(1.07)^{t} \)
The function P gives the estimated number of sea lions in a certain area, where t is the number of years since a study began. What is the best interpretation of P(0) = 1,900 in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The estimated number of sea lions in the area increased by 1,900 each year during the study.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The estimated number of sea lions in the area increased by 107 each year during the study.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The estimated number of sea lions in the area was 1,900 when the study began.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The estimated number of sea lions in the area was 107 when the study began.

questions.whyCorrect: t is measured in years since the study began, so t = 0 is the start of the study and P(0) is the population then. Substituting gives \( 1900(1.07)^{0} = 1900 \), a starting count rather than a rate.

whyWrong.A: 1,900 is the initial population. The yearly change here is multiplicative — a factor of 1.07, or 7 percent — not a fixed addition.
whyWrong.B: 107 is not in the function. The base is 1.07, a multiplier, and multiplying is not the same as adding 107.
whyWrong.D: This misreads the base as the starting value. Putting t = 0 into the equation gives 1,900.

questions.note: Near-identical template to satmath-ma3-exponential-functions-3 (1,200 and 1.06); do not place both in one test.

questions.stem:
y = 5x
y = 2x + 2

How many solutions does the given system of equations have?
questions.whyCorrect: Both equations are in y = mx + b form, so read the slopes straight off: 5 and 2. Two lines with different slopes are not parallel and are not the same line, so they cross exactly once. (Solving confirms it: 5x = 2x + 2 gives \(x = \frac{2}{3}\), a single point.)

whyWrong.B: Two straight lines can meet zero times, once, or infinitely often — never exactly twice. That count only arises with curves.
whyWrong.C: Infinitely many solutions would need the two equations to describe the same line, which requires the same slope and the same y-intercept. Here even the slopes differ.
whyWrong.D: Zero solutions means parallel distinct lines, which requires equal slopes. 5 and 2 are not equal, so the lines must cross.

questions.stem:
\[ y=0.25x^2-6.5x \]
The equation gives the estimated stock price \(y\), in dollars, for a certain company \(x\) days after the company went public, where \(0\le x\le 20\). Which statement is the best interpretation of \((x,y)=(1,58)\) in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: 1 day after the company went public, the company’s estimated stock price is $58.

choices.label: B
choices.content: 58 days after the company went public, the company’s estimated stock price is $1.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The company’s estimated stock price increased $58 every day after the company went public.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The company’s estimated stock price increased $1 every 58 days after the company went public.

questions.whyCorrect: The stem tells you what each variable means: \(x\) is days since going public and \(y\) is the price in dollars. An ordered pair is always (input, output), so \((1,58)\) says that at 1 day the price is $58.

whyWrong.B: The coordinates are swapped. The first number in the pair is \(x\), the number of days.
whyWrong.C: A single point gives one price at one moment, not a rate of change. A constant increase per day would also require a linear model, and this one is quadratic.
whyWrong.D: Same rate-of-change error as C, and with the coordinates swapped as well.

questions.note: The given point does not satisfy the given equation: at x = 1 the equation returns y = -6.25, not 58. The interpretation question is still answerable as printed, but the numbers are internally inconsistent.

questions.stem: A right circular cone has a height of 13 centimeters (cm) and a base with a radius of 6 cm. What is the volume, in \(\text{cm}^3\), of this cone?
questions.whyCorrect: A cone is \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \frac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(13) = \frac{1}{3}\pi(36)(13) = 156\pi\). Square the radius, then take a third.

whyWrong.A: \(26\pi\) is \(2 \times 13\pi\); the base area \(36\pi\) never appears.
whyWrong.B: \(78\pi\) is half of \(156\pi\) — a factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\) was used instead of \(\frac{1}{3}\), or 6 was used instead of \(6^2\).
whyWrong.D: \(468\pi\) is \(\pi r^2 h\), the volume of the cylinder with the same base and height. A cone is a third of that.

questions.stem: The ratio of the internal angles of triangle A is 1:2:3. Triangle B is an equilateral triangle with a side of 12 cm. If the area of triangle A and B are equal and the perimeter of triangle A is \(m\sqrt{2}+n\sqrt{6}\), what is the value of \(m+n\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Angles in the ratio 1:2:3 summing to 180 are 30, 60 and 90, so triangle A is a 30-60-90 triangle with sides \(k\), \(k\sqrt{3}\), \(2k\) and area \(\frac{1}{2}(k)(k\sqrt{3})=\frac{k^{2}\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Triangle B has area \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(12)^{2}=36\sqrt{3}\). Setting them equal gives \(k^{2}=72\), so \(k=6\sqrt{2}\). The perimeter is \(k(1+\sqrt{3}+2)=6\sqrt{2}(3+\sqrt{3})=18\sqrt{2}+6\sqrt{6}\), so m = 18, n = 6 and \(m+n=24\).

whyWrong.A: 6 is n on its own. The question asks for \(m+n\), and m = 18.
whyWrong.B: 12 is the side of the equilateral triangle. You get it as k if you apply the equilateral area formula \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}k^{2}\) to triangle A, but triangle A is a right triangle, so its area is \(\frac{1}{2}\) times the two legs.
whyWrong.C: 18 is m on its own. Add n = 6.

questions.stem:
Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
In quadrilateral KLMN shown, KL = 3, LM = 3, KN = 27, and MN = 27. Diagonals KM and LN (not shown) intersect at point G (not shown), where GK = 1 and GM = 1. If the length of diagonal LN is \(\sqrt{p} + \sqrt{w}\), where p and w are integers, what is the value of \(p + w\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Both L and N are equidistant from K and M, so KLMN is a kite and LN is the perpendicular bisector of KM. That makes triangles LGK and NGK right triangles with leg \(GK = 1\): \(LG = \sqrt{3^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{8}\) and \(NG = \sqrt{27^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{728}\). Since G lies between L and N, \(LN = \sqrt{8} + \sqrt{728}\), so \(p + w = 736\).
questions.note: Figure: quadrilateral KLMN drawn with M top left, N top right, L at the left and K at the bottom; the diagonals are not drawn.
questions.imageAlt: Line drawing of quadrilateral K L M N with M at the upper left, N at the upper right, K at the bottom and L at the left; the diagonals are not drawn.

questions.stem: A hollow steel pipe is in the shape of a right circular cylinder. The steel pipe has an outside diameter of 48 inches, a wall thickness of \(\frac{3}{5}\) inches, and a height of 144 inches. Which of the following is closest to the volume, in cubic inches, of the wall of this steel pipe?
questions.whyCorrect: The wall is the outer cylinder minus the hollow inside. The outer radius is 24 and the inner radius is \(24 - \frac{3}{5} = 23.4\), so the volume is \(\pi\left(24^2 - 23.4^2\right)(144) = \pi(28.44)(144) \approx 12{,}866\) cubic inches. Of the four values offered, only 13,395 is anywhere near that, and the question asks for the closest.

whyWrong.A: Far too small — roughly the size of the ring's cross-sectional area (about 89 square inches) rather than a volume; the 144-inch height was never multiplied in.
whyWrong.B: Also a no-height answer: it is about \(2\pi\) times the thickness times the height, which treats \(\frac{3}{5}\) as the radius of the pipe instead of the thickness of its wall.
whyWrong.C: This drops \(\pi\) and multiplies raw dimensions together; a wall wrapped around a 48-inch-diameter pipe is more than six times this.

questions.note: Exact value is about 12,866 cubic inches; the printed choice 13,395 is roughly 4% high, so the question only works because it asks for the closest value.

questions.stem: The figure above shows a semicircle with the lengths of the adjacent arcs a, a + 1, a + 2, a + 3, and a + 4. If the value of x is 42, what is the value of a?
questions.whyCorrect: Central angles are proportional to the arcs they cut off, and the five arcs make up a semicircle, so their central angles total 180 degrees. The five arcs sum to \(a+(a+1)+(a+2)+(a+3)+(a+4)=5a+10\), and \(x^{\circ}\) is the central angle belonging to the arc of length \(a+4\). So \(\frac{a+4}{5a+10}=\frac{42}{180}\). Cross-multiplying, \(180a+720=210a+420\), giving \(30a=300\) and a = 10. Check: the arcs are 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, totalling 60, and \(\frac{14}{60}(180)=42\).

whyWrong.A: With a = 7 the arcs total 45 and the last arc is 11, giving a central angle of \(\frac{11}{45}(180)=44\), not 42.
whyWrong.B: With a = 8 the arcs total 50 and the last arc is 12, giving \(\frac{12}{50}(180)=43.2\).
whyWrong.C: With a = 9 the arcs total 55 and the last arc is 13, giving \(\frac{13}{55}(180)\approx 42.5\) - close, which is why it is offered, but not exact.

questions.note: Figure needed: a semicircle with centre O on the flat side, divided into five arcs by four radii. Going from the left end of the diameter to the right end the arcs are labelled a, a + 1, a + 2, a + 3, a + 4. The central angle of the last arc (a + 4), nearest the right end of the diameter, is labelled x degrees. Without the figure there is nothing telling the student which arc x belongs to.
questions.imageAlt: A semicircle with its centre marked on the flat side, divided into five adjacent arcs by four radii; each arc carries an algebraic length label and one central angle is labelled in degrees.

questions.stem: In the figure, \(\overline{AC}\) is a diameter of the circle with center O, and AC = 10. Triangle \(\triangle ACB\) is equilateral. The length of BP is n times the length of AO. What is the value of n?
questions.whyCorrect: AO is the radius, 5. Segment BO is the altitude of the equilateral triangle of side 10, so \(BO = \sqrt{10^2 - 5^2} = 5\sqrt{3}\). P lies on the circle along BO, so \(PO = 5\) and \(BP = 5\sqrt{3} - 5\). Dividing by \(AO = 5\) gives \(n = \sqrt{3} - 1\).

whyWrong.A: This mis-simplifies \(\sqrt{75}\) as \(5\sqrt{5}\) instead of \(5\sqrt{3}\) (75 is \(25 \cdot 3\)), and also forgets to cut off the radius.
whyWrong.B: \(\sqrt{3}\) is \(BO \div AO\), the whole altitude. P is on the circle, so the radius \(PO = 5\) still has to be subtracted.
whyWrong.D: This subtracts the radius correctly but carries the same \(\sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{5}\) simplification error.

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, a circle has center D with coordinates \((m, 16)\), where m is a constant. Points E and F lie on the circle. Point E lies on the circle and has coordinates \((m + 4\sqrt{10}, 34)\), and point F has coordinates \((n, 16)\), where n is a constant greater than m. What is the area, in square units, of triangle DEF?
questions.whyCorrect: Get the radius from D to E: \(r = \sqrt{(4\sqrt{10})^2 + (34-16)^2} = \sqrt{160 + 324} = 22\). F has the same y-coordinate as the center, so DF is a horizontal radius of length 22 — use it as the base. The height is the vertical distance from E to the line \(y = 16\), which is \(34 - 16 = 18\). Area \(= \frac{1}{2}(22)(18) = 198\).

whyWrong.B: This uses the horizontal offset \(4\sqrt{10}\) as the base, multiplies by the height 18, and omits the \(\frac{1}{2}\).
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{1}{2}(22)(22)\) — it uses the radius as the height. The height is the vertical drop from E to the base line, which is 18, not 22.
whyWrong.D: The \(\sqrt{10}\) should disappear once the radius is computed; keeping it means the coordinate \(4\sqrt{10}\) was used where the vertical distance 18 belongs.

questions.stem: A right square pyramid has a total surface area of 36,864 square inches, and the combined surface area of the four lateral faces of this pyramid is 20,480 square inches. What is the height, in inches, of this pyramid?
questions.whyCorrect: The base area is the total minus the lateral area: 36,864 − 20,480 = 16,384 square inches, so the base edge is \(\sqrt{16{,}384}=128\) inches. The four lateral faces are triangles with base 128 and height equal to the slant height \(\ell\), so \(4\cdot\frac{1}{2}(128)\ell=256\ell=20{,}480\), giving \(\ell=80\). The slant height, half the base edge and the vertical height form a right triangle, so the height is \(\sqrt{80^{2}-64^{2}}=\sqrt{6400-4096}=\sqrt{2304}=48\).

whyWrong.B: 64 is half the base edge, the horizontal leg of the right triangle, not the vertical height.
whyWrong.C: 80 is the slant height. It is the hypotenuse of the triangle containing the height, so the height must be shorter.
whyWrong.D: 128 is the base edge of the pyramid.

questions.stem: Right rectangular prism X is similar to right rectangular prism Y. The surface area of right rectangular prism X is 59 cm<sup>2</sup>, and the surface area of right rectangular prism Y is 1,475 cm<sup>2</sup>. The volume of right rectangular prism Y is 1,500 cm<sup>3</sup>. What is the sum of the volumes, in cm<sup>3</sup>, of right rectangular prism X and right rectangular prism Y?
questions.whyCorrect: For similar solids, areas scale as the square of the linear ratio and volumes as the cube. The surface areas give \(\frac{1475}{59}=25\), so the linear ratio of Y to X is \(\sqrt{25}=5\). Volumes therefore scale by \(5^{3}=125\), so \(V_{X}=\frac{1500}{125}=12\). The sum is 12 + 1,500 = 1,512. The mistake to avoid is dividing the volume by 25 instead of 125.

Rectangle A2,450490
Rectangle B9,800n
The table gives the areas (square inches) and perimeters (inches) of two similar rectangles, where n is a constant. What is the value of n?
questions.whyCorrect: For similar figures, areas scale by the square of the length ratio while perimeters scale by the ratio itself. Here \(\frac{9800}{2450} = 4\), so the length ratio is \(\sqrt{4} = 2\). The perimeter therefore doubles: \(n = 2(490) = 980\).

whyWrong.B: This applies the area ratio 4 directly to the perimeter. Perimeter is a length, so it scales by 2, not by 4.
whyWrong.C: This uses \(2^3 = 8\), the volume scale factor. These are flat rectangles, so nothing here is cubed.
whyWrong.D: This multiplies the perimeter by 10, which matches no ratio in the problem; \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), not 10.

questions.stem: A circle is inscribed in an equilateral triangle as shown above. Point L is the center of the circle. Points A, B, and C all lie on the circle and the sides of the triangle. The perimeter of the triangle is \(90\sqrt{3}\). The length of arc AC is equal to \(k\pi\). What is the value of k?
questions.whyCorrect: Each side of the equilateral triangle is \(\frac{90\sqrt{3}}{3}=30\sqrt{3}\), and the inradius of an equilateral triangle is \(\frac{s}{2\sqrt{3}}=\frac{30\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{3}}=15\). For the arc you need the central angle ALC. A and C are the points where the circle touches the two sides meeting at vertex Q, and a radius drawn to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the side, so quadrilateral QALC has two right angles and its angle at Q is 60 degrees; the remaining angle ALC is 360 − 90 − 90 − 60 = 120 degrees. The arc is therefore \(\frac{120}{360}\cdot 2\pi(15)=10\pi\), so k = 10.
questions.note: Figure needed: an equilateral triangle PQR with P at the top, Q at the lower left and R at the lower right, and its inscribed circle centred at L. A is the point of tangency on side PQ, B the point of tangency on side PR, and C the point of tangency on side QR. Arc AC is the minor arc, the one on the Q side that does not contain B.
questions.imageAlt: An equilateral triangle P Q R with a circle inscribed in it; the centre of the circle is marked L and the three points where the circle touches the sides are marked A, B and C.

questions.stem: \[5x^{2}-40px+5y^{2}+70py=325p^{2}\]In the xy-plane, the graph of the given equation is a circle, where p is a constant. The center of the circle is (-8, 14). If a square is inscribed in the circle, what is the area of the square?
questions.whyCorrect: Divide by 5 first: \(x^{2}-8px+y^{2}+14py=65p^{2}\). Completing the square gives \((x-4p)^{2}+(y+7p)^{2}=65p^{2}+16p^{2}+49p^{2}=130p^{2}\), so the center is \((4p,\,-7p)\). Matching to (-8, 14) gives p = -2 from either coordinate, so \(r^{2}=130(-2)^{2}=520\). For a square inscribed in a circle the diagonal is the diameter, \(2r\), so the side is \(\frac{2r}{\sqrt{2}}=r\sqrt{2}\) and the area is \(2r^{2}=2(520)=1040\). You never need r itself, only \(r^{2}\).

questions.stem: In triangle DEF, angle F is a right angle, point Q lies on DE, point J lies on EF, and QJ is parallel to DF. If the length of EF is 45 units, the length of FJ is 24 units, and the area of triangle DEF is 630 square units, what is the perimeter of triangle QEJ, in units?
questions.whyCorrect: The right angle is at F, so the legs are DF and EF: \(\frac{1}{2}(DF)(45)=630\) gives DF = 28, and the hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{28^{2}+45^{2}}=\sqrt{2809}=53\), so triangle DEF has perimeter 28 + 45 + 53 = 126. Since QJ is parallel to DF, triangle QEJ is similar to triangle DEF, and the matching sides along EF give the ratio. J is 24 from F, so EJ = 45 − 24 = 21 and the ratio is \(\frac{21}{45}=\frac{7}{15}\). Perimeters scale by the same ratio: \(\frac{7}{15}(126)=\frac{294}{5}\).

whyWrong.B: This is half of 126, which is what you get by treating J as the midpoint of EF. FJ = 24 and EJ = 21 are close but not equal, and the ratio is \(\frac{21}{45}\), not \(\frac{1}{2}\).
whyWrong.C: This scales the perimeter 126 by \(\frac{7}{10}\) instead of \(\frac{7}{15}\) - the similarity ratio read off the wrong pair of corresponding sides. The side of the small triangle along EF is EJ = 21, and it corresponds to the whole of EF = 45.
whyWrong.D: 126 is the perimeter of the large triangle DEF. Triangle QEJ is the small one cut off near vertex E.

questions.stem: In the figure above, what is the length of NQ?
questions.whyCorrect: Triangle MNP is right-angled at N with legs 3 and 4, so \(MP = 5\). The area can be written two ways: \(\frac{1}{2}(3)(4)\) using the legs, or \(\frac{1}{2}(MP)(NQ)\) using the hypotenuse and the altitude to it. Setting them equal gives \(NQ = \frac{3 \cdot 4}{5} = 2.4\).

whyWrong.A: There is no computation here that gives 2.2; it is a near-miss for a student measuring the figure instead of using the area relation.
whyWrong.B: Same trap as A — the altitude is exactly \(\frac{12}{5}\), so a value of 2.3 means the relationship was estimated rather than computed.
whyWrong.D: 2.5 is half the hypotenuse, which is the length of the median from N to MP. NQ is perpendicular to MP, and in a non-isosceles right triangle the altitude and the median are different segments.

questions.note: Figure: triangle MNP with the right angle at N, MN = 3, NP = 4, and Q the foot of the perpendicular from N to MP.

questions.stem: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle with a radius of 8 inches. What is the area of the region that lies within the circle but outside the triangle, in square inches?
questions.whyCorrect: The circle's area is \(\pi(8)^2 = 64\pi\). For an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius R, the side is \(R\sqrt{3} = 8\sqrt{3}\), so the triangle's area is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(8\sqrt{3})^2 = 48\sqrt{3}\). (Same result from three central triangles: \(3 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(8)^2\sin 120^\circ\).) The leftover region is \(64\pi - 48\sqrt{3}\).

whyWrong.B: This is half the triangle's area. The triangle's height is \(R + \frac{R}{2} = 12\), not 6 — the center sits two-thirds of the way along each median, not at the midpoint.
whyWrong.C: \(32\sqrt{3}\) comes from a side of \(8\sqrt{2}\), the relation for an inscribed square. For an equilateral triangle the side is \(R\sqrt{3}\).
whyWrong.D: Every term here is a quarter of the correct one, which is what you get by treating 8 as the diameter and using a radius of 4.

questions.note: The stem says to round to the nearest tenth, but all four choices are exact expressions; the rounding instruction is left over from another version of the question.

questions.stem: A club plans to sell tote bags. The club members estimate they will sell 80 tote bags when the bags are priced at $9 each. For every price increase of $1, they estimate they will sell 8 fewer bags. What is the estimated revenue, in dollars, when the bags are priced at $12 each? (revenue = price × number of bags sold)
questions.whyCorrect: Count the price increases first: going from $9 to $12 is 3 increases of $1. Each one costs 8 bags of sales, so the estimated number sold is \(80 - 3(8) = 56\). Revenue is price times quantity: \(12 \times 56 = 672\). The common slip is to use 80 bags at the new price, or to subtract 8 only once.

questions.stem: A batch of smoothies consists of 4 cups of milk and 2 bananas and has 1,228 milligrams (mg) of calcium. There is 304 mg of calcium in 1 cup of milk. How much calcium, in mg, is in 1 banana?
questions.whyCorrect: The milk supplies \(4 \times 304 = 1{,}216\) mg, so the bananas supply \(1{,}228 - 1{,}216 = 12\) mg. That 12 mg is for two bananas, so one banana has 6 mg — the last division is the step most people skip.

whyWrong.B: 12 mg is the calcium in both bananas together. Divide by 2 for one banana.
whyWrong.C: This is roughly \(\frac{1{,}228 - 304}{2}\) — you subtracted the calcium in one cup of milk instead of all four.
whyWrong.D: This is the calcium in the milk, \(4 \times 304\), not in a banana.

questions.stem:
3x2 + x − 5 = 0

What is the greatest solution to the given equation?
questions.whyCorrect: Use the quadratic formula with \(a=3\), \(b=1\), \(c=-5\): the discriminant is \(1^2-4(3)(-5)=61\), so \(x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{61}}{6}=-\frac{1}{6}\pm\frac{\sqrt{61}}{6}\). The greatest solution takes the plus sign.

whyWrong.A: This is the same pair of solutions but with the minus sign — it is the smaller root, not the greater.
whyWrong.C: The denominator is \(2a=6\), not 3. Dividing by 3 comes from using \(a\) instead of \(2a\).
whyWrong.D: Same denominator error as C: \(2a=6\), so both terms need a 6 underneath.

questions.stem: \[b - 19 = \frac{x}{y}\]The given equation relates the positive numbers b, x, and y. Which equation correctly expresses x in terms of b and y?
questions.whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by y to get x on its own: \(y(b-19) = x\). Distributing the y across both terms gives \(x = by - 19y\). The 19 is inside the parentheses, so it gets a y as well.

whyWrong.A: This divides by y when the correct move is to multiply — x is already being divided by y.
whyWrong.C: This multiplies by y and then divides by y, which returns you to where you started.
whyWrong.D: This attaches the y to b only. Multiplying a difference by y multiplies both parts of it.

questions.stem: An auditorium has seats for 3,200 people. Tickets to attend a show at the auditorium currently cost $8.00. For each $1.00 increase to the ticket price, 100 fewer tickets will be sold. This situation can be modeled by the equation \( -100x^{2} + 2{,}400x = 25{,}600 \) where x represents the increase in ticket price, in dollars, and y represents the revenue, in dollars, from ticket sales. If the equation is graphed in the xy-plane, at what value of x is the maximum of the graph?
questions.whyCorrect: Revenue is price times tickets sold: \( (8 + x)(3200 - 100x) = -100x^{2} + 2{,}400x + 25{,}600 \) . A parabola with a negative leading coefficient peaks at its vertex, and the vertex is at \( x = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{2400}{2(-100)} = 12 \) . The constant term does not move the vertex left or right, so you only need a and b.

whyWrong.A: 32 is 3,200 divided by 100, the number of $1 increases that would drop sales to zero. Revenue is already falling long before that.
whyWrong.C: 24 is \( -\frac{b}{a} \) , which forgets the 2 in the vertex formula. It is the second x-intercept of the revenue curve above its starting level, not the peak.
whyWrong.D: 8 is the current ticket price, not an increase. x counts dollars added to that price.

questions.note: The printed model reads "-100x^2 + 2,400x = 25600" and then refers to a y that never appears; it should read y = -100x^2 + 2,400x + 25,600, which is what (8 + x)(3200 - 100x) expands to. The vertex is at x = 12 either way.

questions.stem:
2x = 20y − 8

One of the two equations in a system of linear equations is given. The system has no solution. Which equation could be the second equation in this system?
questions.whyCorrect: Reduce the given equation: dividing 2x = 20y − 8 by 2 gives x = 10y − 4. For no solution you need the same x-to-y relationship with a different constant. Multiply choice B by 2 and you get x = 10y — the same coefficient 10 on y, but constant 0 rather than −4 — so the lines are parallel and never meet.

whyWrong.A: The coefficient on y is 5, not 10, so this line has a different slope and crosses the given line at exactly one point.
whyWrong.C: This is the given equation divided by 2, so it is the same line. That produces infinitely many solutions, not none.
whyWrong.D: Multiplying by 2 gives x = 20y − 8, whose y-coefficient is 20 rather than 10. Different slope, so the system has exactly one solution.

questions.stem: Which expression is a factor of \(7x^2-9x+14x-18\) ?
questions.whyCorrect: The expression is deliberately left unsimplified so you can factor by grouping. Group the first two terms and the last two: \(x(7x-9)+2(7x-9)=(7x-9)(x+2)\). The two factors are \(7x-9\) and \(x+2\), and only \(7x-9\) is offered.

whyWrong.A: The second factor is \(x+2\), not \(x-2\); you flipped the sign of the constant pulled out of \(14x-18\).
whyWrong.B: Nothing produces \(x+9\); the 9 belongs to the grouped factor \(7x-9\), attached to \(7x\), not to \(x\).
whyWrong.D: You paired the 7 with the 2 from the wrong grouping. Grouping gives \(7x-9\) and \(x+2\), never \(7x+2\); check by expanding \((7x+2)\) against the \(-18\) constant.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by \( f(x) = 4x^{2} \) . What is the value of \( f(11) \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Square the input first, then multiply by 4. \( 11^{2} = 121 \) and \( 4 \times 121 = 484 \) . The 4 is a coefficient, so it is not squared along with the x.

whyWrong.A: 44 is 4 × 11, which ignores the exponent entirely.
whyWrong.B: 52 does not come from any correct step. If you got it, check that you squared 11 before multiplying by 4.
whyWrong.C: 88 doubles the input instead of squaring it: \( 4 \times 11 \times 2 \) . Squaring means 11 × 11, not 11 × 2.
